Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order as my party's communications critic and a member of the communications and culture committee of the House of Commons.
John Kim Bell is a distinguished Canadian. He is the first North American native to become a symphony conductor and he is founder and president of the Canadian Native Arts Foundation, which provides educational grants and scholarships for promising young natives.
I can testify to the fact that he has been applying to appear before the House of Commons committee on communications and culture to be heard with respect to funding for native cultural projects. There has been some resistance to allowing him to appear before the committee.
He is quoted in the Ottawa Citizen today as saying with respect to the hon. member who is the Chair of that committee, that the Chair said, "The problem is, Indians are lazy." These were his exact words. These are the words of the Chair of the committee to Mr. John Kim Bell. There is a very serious allegation of racism and it comes at a time when there are some unfortunate similarities of racist attitudes in other issues in other parts of the country.
I put the government on notice that we expect a statement from the Minister of Communications or from the Prime Minister with respect to this matter.

The House resumed from Friday, January 26, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bouchard (Roberval) that Bill C-5, an act to amend the Railway Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, I will just take a couple of minutes to make one point on this legislation. The transportation policy over the years has been based on the need for transportation, particularly in remote areas. What is happening today is that transportation policy is becoming less of a national policy and one more based on economics, the amount of money that can be made. This why I want to make one

February 9, 1990
Government Orders
point on this particular shortline railway, the Central Western Railway bill.
This railway is an experiment. The basis on which the movement of grain can be paid for has not changed because this railway is in place. It is an experiment. Any grain that would be delivered from any point to Vancouver or to Thunder Bay, would get the same amount of freight as if it were transported from the end of the railway. In other words, there is no basic method, except for government subsidies, to pay for the continuing operation of this railway.
The $7 million used to operate this railway is entirely a government subsidy. Those funds which I gather amount to some $17 million after upgrading are of no real value in changing the arrangements for the movement of grain. They are a slight saving to the CNR, and of course they are a saving to the farmers on that line because they would have to haul many more miles if the line were abandoned.
We should recognize that the funds to keep this railway or any other shortline railway within the structure we presently have will require the subsidy of the government for its entire operation. That is the way it will operate unless a change is made in the movement of grain by this government.

The House resumed from Thursday, January 25, consideration of the motion of Mr. Clark (Yellowhead) that Bill C-25, An Act to amend the Geneva Conventions Act, the National Defence Act and the Trademarks Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

I was
speaking to this bill when it was before the House a week
or so ago. The point I was trying to make at that time was that although it is very important to have the Geneva Convention and the protocols ratified, there are other things we should be doing to make sure that the world is a better place and that there is less chance of war.
Making rules for making war less barbaric, although recognized as necessary, really gives us the idea that war is okay. Therefore even as we ratify the protocols that are part of the Geneva Convention, we should do things that will help to make the world more likely to keep the peace.
I want to mention a few of the things I think Canada can do to increase the likelihood of peace around the world. Something we could do immediately here right at home is ban the testing of weapons in Canada. We could eliminate testing of the cruise missile tomorrow if we wished. That in itself would send a message that we are really concerned about making peace possible in the world.
We could establish a comprehensive test ban and Canada could press for such a ban. The 1963 treaty banning the atmospheric testing of nuclear warheads was a move in that direction. We can thank Howard Green, who was the minister at that time, for his significant contribution to the ban on testing nuclear weapons in the atmosphere.
We now have U.S. resistance to a comprehensive ban on the testing of nuclear weapons. But Canada could do something about that by refusing to be part of it. Instead, we are going along with the strategic defence initiative, the star wars initiative, that the U.S. has in place. By being part of that star wars initiative we are contributing to the development of armaments in the world. We are therefore part of the resistance, if you wish, that the U.S. has shown to the testing of nuclear weapons.
We should consider all of the money we are spending on armaments in conjunction with the money being spent on other things happening around the world.
Over 20 million people have died in wars since 1945. The world spends $130 million every hour on armaments. During that same hour 2,000 children die of starvation and disease.
The transfer of arms to Third World countries has risen from $5 billion per year in the early 1970s to as high as $35 billion per year in the 1980s. Many of those arms transfers are done on credit, something which adds to the debt of Third World countries. Consequently, this
February 9, 1990

decreases the possibility of worthwhile development and the elimination of hunger and disease in those countries.
There have been some positive developments, and Canada has a good record of development aid. However, our record is not as good as it could be and we could do more. We could do more in terms of peacekeeping work and development. As I mentioned the other day, we could also make a very basic and direct move by reducing our military exports.
When this government first came to power five years ago, one of its first privatization operations concerned the armaments industry in Canada. While the armaments industry was under public control we had very specific control over the export of those armaments. Since that time-and I cannot blame the company that took over the manufacture of armaments too greatly- arms made in Canada have been appearing all over the world.
According to Project Ploughshares, approximately 300 million armaments from Canada go to the Third World either directly or as parts of units assembled elsewhere. A large number of the recipient countries that are serious violators of human rights.
In the Iran-Iraq war, Canadian-made components for weapons appeared on both sides. There should be stronger restrictions so that, minimally, military and military-related products do not go to human rights violators. The end use of any components should be part of the exporting requirements and should be firmly controlled. Better still, we should stop making and selling armaments completely.
Canadians could also make an effort, both nationally and internationally, to reduce the flow of weapons on the international market. As a place to start we could make requirements which would force suppliers to recognize when they are contributing to world armament.
We could appeal to places such as Indo-China, the Horn of Africa, South Africa, Central America, the Middle East and other places where there is widespread killing, devastation and injustice. We could deal with
Government Orders
them and start a movement toward the elimination of armaments.
Even as we make rules for war we should be doing much more to ensure that war becomes less likely in the world.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: On questions or comments, the hon. member for Kamloops.

Mr. Speaker, I have a short question for my hon. colleague who has spoken so thoughtfully regarding Bill C-25. We are aware that the legislation deals with international conventions. From time to time one asks why we bother to sign these conventions if we are going to ignore them.
The Canadian government supported the American invasion of Panama which was in direct contravention of the international principles of national sovereignty as articulated in the United Nations Charter to which, of course, we are a signatory. Does that not put into question the whole matter of living up to these international conventions that we sign?
I suppose we could also draw attention to the situation in East Timor. Again, despite the United Nations Charter's recognition of the rights of the people to self determination, the Canadian government continues to refuse to recognize this right in practice when it comes to the case of East Timor.
I had the opportunity some time back to actually be one of the visitors to East Timor. As a result of that visit there were some unfortunate comments that all is well. Despite all of the evidence that was presented regarding Indonesia's invasion of East Timor in the late 1970s and the fact that Indonesia has continued to occupy East Timor ever since we have really never had any comment from the federal government. It is simply ignoring the plight of the people of East Timor.
We could talk about the issue of the CANDU reactors and nuclear proliferation when we see our sale of CANDU reactors to regimes like those in Cambodia, South Korea, and India. Obviously this has implications in terms of nuclear proliferation in contravention of the principles of the non-proliferation treaty.
There are so many conventions that we have signed, yet one could provide a whole list of where the Canadian government ignores the fact that we are a signator to these conventions. I think particularly economically

February 9, 1990
Government Orders
about asbestos when the International Labour Organization has laid very clear restrictions on the sale and use of it yet we send tons and tons to countries like Thailand.
I wonder if my hon. friend would comment on some of these questions and the fact that, while we give lip service to international conventions, when the crunch comes we seem to often turn a blind eye. Does he agree with that, and what would he suggest we could do as a result of that?

Mr. Speaker, Canada is not lily-white in any way when it comes to making itself considered around the world as a peace-loving nation. We do have a considerable reputation as a peace-keeping nation, but we continue to support a variety of actions which belie the seriousness of our seeming desire to be seen as a peace-loving nation.
I spoke earlier about the hypocrisy of Canada in these areas. It is not something that we should dwell on because it is something that every nation in the world can be accused of. Even as we say that we want to eliminate war, we establish rules under which wars can be carried out and, therefore, seem to legitimize the war. At the same time we build, sell and trade armaments. We force countries into debt by giving them armaments on a credit basis. Our reason for this is, if we do not do it somebody else will. It is a pretty thin excuse.
The areas of export and indirect violation of human rights to which Canada contributes are all part of that hypocrisy. I want to stress the point that we are one of the nations that can be accused of that. We are not the only nation but we can lead the way in eliminating many of those things which do contribute to war, devastation and hunger, and in doing so perhaps make the world a better and more peaceful place to live.

The House resumed from Monday, December 18, consideration of the motion of Mr. Epp that Bill C-44, an act respecting the Hibernia Development Project and to amend certain acts in relation thereto, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, I rise as my party's former energy critic. I started out going right up the National Energy Program and then right down the National Energy Program. I was there as it was brought in and as it was dismantled, and we are back to square one. We are not really back to square one. There have been some major changes in energy and I would like to speak briefly about that in addressing this bill.
This bill concerns the financing of the Hibernia energy megaproject; drilling for oil in iceberg alley, as they call it, hundreds of kilometres off Newfoundland in the Atlantic ocean. This bill, C-44, runs parallel to another bill, C-45, which is to finance what is called the OSLO project, which is a project in the Alberta tar sands, another vast energy megaproject.
As Canadians we must ask ourselves whether Canada's energy future lies with big hydrocarbon megaprojects. Consider that last year Canada spewed 473 million tonnes of carbon dioxide into our atmosphere. The carbon era, the era that powered our society and powered our motor vehicles especially through gasoline from oil, I believe is coming to a close. Part of our problem, to be fair, is that we are in an interstitial period, a kind of interim period. We still drive cars. We have not adjusted to the new reality of the world environment.
Scientists are telling us the carbon dioxide that is produced from the burning of fossil fuels is producing, together with other greenhouse gases, a global warming by trapping the infrared radiation in the atmosphere. There have been all sorts of dire predictions: melting ice caps, rising sea levels and changing weather. We all seem to notice changing weather, but is it real, are the predictions real? We do not know, but we would be foolish not to take seriously the prediction of scientists.
February 9, 1990

I am told by some of my friends and some professionals in the area that all bets are off, that, as David Suzuki said, we have ten years to save this planet. So we have to look at these vast projects in a new way. We have to look at them as environmentalists as well as energy producers. I think that members on all sides of the House realize that, including people from Alberta and people from Newfoundland who want to benefit from the projects.
There is a second reality we have to face. One of the news headlines this morning reads: "Get ready for harsh budget, Tories warn". We are going to have a budget on February 20 and I suspect that we are going to be told how we have to cut the deficit and how difficult it is to run a modern government, how there will have to be cutbacks in certain programs. That is one of the reasons we are getting the goods and services tax, to pay for government expenditures.
I want the House to look at the expenditures here in Hibernia because they are very illustrative of how expensive these projects are. This bill talks about a grant. Do not forget that there are some of the biggest oil companies in the world involved here, but we have to give them a grant. We have to cut back on giving grants to welfare families, single mothers and so on with kids. That is welfare, but this is not welfare, this is a grant to Exxon, Imperial Oil, Shell and Mobil, the biggest companies in the world. We are giving a grant for the defraying of capital costs in the amount of $1.04 billion. As well we are taking up loan guarantees on the capital project of up to $1.66 billion.
That's a loan.

Well, Mr. Speaker, do you get a loan guarantee on your mortgage from the government? Do you get a loan guarantee when you go to the bank? Not likely. The government is giving a direct loan in the amount of $300 million, loan guarantees for what is called a temporary financing facility in the amount of $175 million and interest payable guarantees on the $1.66 billion loan guarantee. In other words, if the loan is defaulted, the government has guaranteed that not only will we pay the principle, we will pick up the interest charges as well. Not a bad deal for the international oil companies.
So we are talking about a direct expenditure, a grant of up to $1.04 billion, a $300 million loan, and various and sundry loan guarantees and interest guarantees in the
Government Orders
amount of $1,835 billion. That is a total possible government investment of $3,139 billion. That is a tidy sum in anybody's book.
Talk about the jobs.

I will come to the jobs. The fact is this is the price that we are paying for hydrocarbon fuels. You can make the argument that we have to have the insurance of having fuels. There is also a suspicion that governments tend to win elections with promises. Projects and megaprojects are among the famous ones: Bourassa, James Bay; the Conservatives and the Liberals before them, Hibernia; the Tories promising the upgrad-er in Lethbridge and the tar sands project.
I am hearing from the hon. members from Alberta across the way. I am just saying that it costs a lot of money. We are saying to Canadians that we are going to have a tough budget, we are going to have to cut back, we are going to have to pull the purse strings in, yet look at the money that is going to feed this beast, and it is a beast. It is the hydrocarbon beast.
There are alternatives, but before I come to them I would like to talk about the OSLO project. I have just said there is $3.1 billion in the Hibernia project.
It will not go ahead unless it is economically sound.

The member says it will not go ahead unless it is economically sound. It is only going ahead because the Government of Canada is putting up the guarantees. It is not the market. The private companies will not do this of their own accord. They want and have received government guarantees. This is not free enterprise.
Let me deal with OSLO. I am trying to be fair. I have already said that we need gasoline. We are still riding in a carbon society, still feeding the beast. OSLO is the megaproject in Alberta. We are talking about a grant for capital costs of up to $425 million and a price of oil production subsidy of $48 million.
I will be consistent. When I was energy critic I advocated a price floor in difficult times and a price ceiling in times that were too easy for the industry and it was creaming it off. But this is what is happening in this project. It is a regulation and it is providing a no-lose situation to the private entrepreneurs who are making

February 9, 1990
Government Orders
this project go basically. That is a pretty good deal and it is pretty costly to the Canadian public.
We are looking at a $48 million floor guarantee, $425 million in capital cost start-up and loan guarantees of up to $642 million. If you add that up we are looking at another $1.4 billion. So now we are up to $5 billion in two projects. That is billion, not million. This is at a time when the headlines are saying: "Get ready for harsh budget, Tories warn",, and the GST is coming in to put a 7 per cent sales tax all across the country. This is what Canadians are paying for and Canadians should know that.
Let us talk about the environment for a moment. It seems to me that there is another energy future we should be looking at.
Nuclear.

At the Montreal conference and other conferences there has been a target set for a 20 per cent reduction in carbon dioxide emissions by the year 2005. We are going to need special measures to do that. Now where is the money coming from for that? Here is $5 billion for two megaprojects. The government has cut back on its research into alternate energy measures and we are spending something like $49 million on research and development in energy conservation.
There have been studies which go back ten years. Amoiy Lovins, in Hard Energy Paths, says that nuclear, coal and hydro big energy projects are no longer appropriate. The nuclear industry is pushing hard to come in because it says it does not produce acid rain or greenhouse gasses and so on. The problem is that we do not have any reliable way of disposing of nuclear waste. It is immoral for this generation to hand nuclear waste to a future generation, with vast clean-up costs. People are starting to understand the cost of the environment.
I will give an example. My hon. colleague from Esquimalt knows that recently the government of British Columbia sold land in downtown Vancouver, the old Expo land, to Li Ki-shing of Hong Kong for $100 million. Then it received a bill, which may exceed what they got for the land, to clean up the old industrial wastes in the land. There are a lot of costs out there. People are now environmentally conscious. We are trying to save this planet. We should not be putting $5 billion into megaprojects.
Lovins says that we have to look at alternate ways of getting away from the beast. I think we all agree with that. He says that we should be encouraging hydrogen fuels, which are currently being wasted.
As an example, one pipeline in Alberta is venting off $360 million a year in unused hydrogen. We have to start getting into the 21st century a little ahead of time. We have to use the hydrogen.
Hydrogen can be made with surplus electricity and at sites of natural gas extraction so we can use the Alberta natural gas. Hydrogen creates water vapour when it is burned. It is a good transportation fuel. Now is also the time when we have to retrofit all isolated communities with solar, wind or small-scale hydro projects. We have known this for years but now the reality is coming in. We cannot feed this beast any more. We have to come up with alternate energy paths, not $5 billion into a vast megaproject.
I want to address the project itself. This bill provides inadequate job guarantees for Newfoundlanders for the public money that it is spending. Many members of the House who are not from Newfoundland, that wonderful province, travel there. It seems to me that for so many years people in Atlantic Canada have been led down the garden path or, if I can mix the metaphor, have been led to believe that there is a pot of gold at the rainbow. There is always a pot of gold at the end of that rainbow and Hibernia is the latest. It is suddenly going to turn a have-not province into a have province.
We all sympathize with that, especially people from western Canada. The former premier, my friend from Esquimalt, made the gas industry in British Columbia into a public marketing agency and used our resource to pump hundreds of millions of dollars into the provincial budget and then redistributed that money to the people of the province. That was good government. So we westerners know how to use heritage funds and we sympathize.
Let us not lead Atlantic Canadians down the garden path. Let us not put out Hibernia, with all the money going into it, as a project that will suddenly turn a have-not province into a have province. The real future of a province like Newfoundland is still in the harvesting of the fisheries.
In my view, for the public money that goes into Hibernia, the bill still does not guarantee jobs for native Newfoundlanders. I submit that when the committee is considering this bill it should look at what was done by
February 9, 1990

the Scots in Aberdeen and how they managed to get jobs for local people there.
Look at what the Norwegians do. Look at the requirements. Somehow the Canadian government has a mind fix that we cannot require jobs for Canadians because that is against the international marketing system. Look at the way the Brits did it with the North Sea oil and the way the Norwegians did it. They were much more sophisticated than we are. They guaranteed jobs for their people.
I say this bill provides inadequate job opportunities for Newfoundlanders in terms of the public money that is going into the project.
Second, putting so much money into one project will inevitably take away other moneys that could go to Atlantic Canada for economic diversification. That is what Atlantic Canada needs, not one big energy megaproject but a number of projects that can work with the resources in Atlantic Canada.
The government says it will leave that up to the market. If you read the speech made on December 18, 1989, in this House by the energy critic of the New Democratic Party, the hon. member for Edmonton East, sets out in detail the cost of this project, the fact that jobs have to be guaranteed and the fact that there has to be other economic diversification for Atlantic Canada. If we do not say that to the people of Atlantic Canada we are not telling them the truth. We are saying that Hibernia is the pot of gold at the end of the rainbow and it just does not fit in.
I want to return to the environment briefly before I conclude. As I said, Canadians have added a new criterion to deciding on energy projects and that is the environment. We are requiring, and the courts are requiring now, that every project be looked at in terms of its environmental impact and so on. This project in Hibernia will have to be looked at in that regard. There are some vast dangers out there.
We think of the icebergs out there and remember the Ocean Ranger oil rig. I remember being in the House when the minister stood up on that very sad day and announced the loss of those workers on that oil rig. It is a very dangerous area. When you have an accident it is
Government Orders
pretty hard to cap things 400 miles out in the Atlantic Ocean off Newfoundland.
One has to go back to the Brundtland report, the United Nations report which is now in the forefront of our criterion for considering environmental projects. Brundtland said, in Our Common Energy Futures, choosing an energy strategy inevitably means choosing an environmental strategy. That is the key.
Dare I quote the Prime Minister? He said at the Changing Atmosphere Conference in Toronto: "The world is coming to recognize what we believe to be self-evident, that development and environmental protection are mutually enforcing, not mutually exclusive. Our economic activity must be increasingly compatible with today's environmental facts of life."
Here is an energy megaproject, with is over $3 billion in loans, guarantees and so on, at a time when we do not have much money in this country. Is that where we should be putting our money? Is this the way to deal with carbon in the atmosphere? Are there no other alternatives?
We in the New Democratic Party believe in the greening of Canada and the greening of the world. We are going to deal with these projects and these bills with questions and comments in the House of Commons from the point of view of being a newer, greener party.
I would like to move an amendment to the motion, seconded by the hon. member from Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca. I move:
That the motion for second reading and reference to the Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources of Bill C-44, an act respecting the Hibernia Development Project and to amend certain acts in relation thereto, be amended by deleting all the words after the word "That" and substituting the following:
Be it resolved that Bill C-44, an act respecting the Hibernia Development Project and to amend certain Acts in relation thereto be not now read a second time because:
(1)	this House is of the opinion that simply giving huge amounts of money away to any private sector development without securing equivalent equity in such project for the people of Canada is wrong in principle;
(2)	this House is of the opinion that pursuing further fossil fuel megaprojects in the absence of concerted government action to reduce C02 emissions in Canada generally is wrong in principle; and,
(3)	this House is of the opinion that proceeding with the Hibernia project in the absence of sufficient guarantees of consequent job opportunities and economic development prospects for the people

Government Orders
of Newfoundland and Labrador and of the Atlantic region generally, is wrong in principle.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the member a sequence of questions. I will ask them all together. They are three very short questions.
First, would private enterprise have gone ahead with this had the guarantees and the government assistance not been in place? Second, could the member give us any indication of what the price per barrel of oil would have to be for private enterprise to have gone it on their own? And third, does it mean that indirectly, or directly if you wish, we are guaranteeing that price per barrel to the corporations that do go into this project?

Mr. Speaker, the member's question is exactly on point. It depends. Private enterprise would not go into this alone because the price of oil is too low. I never could get out of the Minister of Energy, even with repeated questions when I was energy critic, what market price for a barrel of oil was required for Hibernia to be economically viable without government subsidization. They said it was between $30 and $50 a barrel.
That's too high. You know that.

Well, we do not know whether it's high or low. Certainly the price of oil right now is too low and so we have a government subsidized project, which still may

not go ahead. The hon. member is right. In fact, the government is guaranteeing the project and guaranteeing an economic price for the project.

Mr. Speaker, Supreme Court Justice Bertha Wilson has made a statement of profound importance to relationships between men and women and to the very foundation of our values as a society. She is right when she says our laws and judicial system discriminate against women and that they fail to respond to women's values of mutual obligations, caring for one another and preserving relationships.
She has put her finger on the root cause of pervasive injustice against women and children, the reason courts treat theft more seriously than wife beating or child abuse, why court ordered support payments leave mothers and children in poverty and then are ignored in 85 per cent of the cases, and why governments can play games with pay equity and pension justice even for its own employees.
To paraphrase Justice Wilson, it is impossible for men to respond even conceptually to the vulnerability women feel because it is outside the realm of their personal experience. Canadian society cannot wait while women make their way in equal numbers into the Parliaments and courts to change this system. We will only be the richer if our government acts-

Mr. Speaker, a recent survey of my constituents revealed that 63
per cent of respondents felt that the Meech Lake Accord was important for Quebec and Canada, while only 16 per cent disagreed. Twenty-one per cent of respondents indicated they had no opinion.
Mr. Speaker, the results of this survey show that the people of Temiscamingue care about Meech Lake and want the Accord to be ratified so that Quebec will grow within our Canadian federation.
Mr. Speaker, I also see a very clear message to opponents of Meech Lake that they should weigh carefully the consequences of their actions in the months to come, if they do not want to jeopardise the unity of this country.
History might judge them very harshly. Yes to Meech Lake means yes to Quebec and yes to Canada, and it means saying yes to a country that is stronger because it is more united.

Mr. Speaker, I want to draw to the attention of the House the latest in the government's campaign to sell the universally unpopular goods and services tax.
Canadians are already being bombarded with a $14 million GST propaganda campaign. Now the ultimate in insults arrives in the 1989 tax guide, a GST insert that is purely a propaganda tool.
The insert states that the GST will reduce the deficit, but the Minister of Finance has repeatedly claimed that the GST will be revenue neutral. It states that the GST will make a fairer tax system, yet the GST is regressive and hurts lower and middle income earners.
The insert states that the GST will pay for social programs, but this government continues to reduce social spending. It states the GST will help lower and modest income earners, but seniors and the poor simply do not believe this.
Surely a person filling out an income tax return should be protected from the Mulroney government's political hypocrisy. Can this government not at least let people do their incpme tax in peace?

February 9, 1990

Mr. Speaker, these are challenging and stimulating days to be a Canadian. We are living the historic reality of building our nation Canada and we must build it together in our two official founding languages and in our many ethnic cultures. For me, that is the essence of being a Canadian.
To achieve true understanding about our diverse identity and to generate the kind of tolerance and mutual respect which Canadian unity will demand, we must constantly strive to know one another.
In my riding of Fredericton today, a small citizens' committee on language and culture is meeting regularly to encourage continuing dialogue between English and French neighbours. It is succeeding, slowly but surely, to enhance a spirit of common cause among its members which will spread throughout our city.
From such small candles, larger lights will glow. I recommend similar initiatives for true communication among Canadians in every community across this country.

Mr. Speaker, in the past week or two there has been a lot of talk about the cost of bilingualism. What are the facts?
The whole federal bilingualism program costs less than one-half of 1 per cent of total federal spending.
Again, one-half of 1 per cent is the total amount for the whole federal bilingualism program, including contributions to help the provinces deliver minority language education and services.
The new Ontario French Language Services program entails no costs whatsoever for municipalities. Moreover, the Ontario government estimates that it will spend about $11 million a year to deliver this new program. This is about three one-hundredths of 1 per cent of Ontario's total spending.
To put it another way, federal bilingualism program costs every Canadian man, woman and child 6 cents per day.
The new Ontario program will cost each resident of Ontario three tenths of a penny per day. Add the federal and Ontario programs and you get six and one-third cents per day for each Ontario resident. Is an investment of six and one-third cents per day too much to keep our country together?

Mr. Speaker, our Canada is a great country and Canadians are a capable and creative people.
On Wednesday night of this week I was privileged to join with some distinguished Canadians, including members from both sides of this House, at the Museum of Civilization for the premier showing of an all-Canadian film Divided Loyalties, the story of Joseph Brant. This 100 per cent Canadian film is a tribute to a great Canadian loyalist. Produced by Baton Productions and Mr. Tom Gould, it is an example of the quality that can be created by Canadians. The film is a tribute to the actors, technicians and financiers, all of whom are Canadian. They deserve congratulations for an excellent production.

Mr. Speaker, this week Moose Jaw Packers was forced to stop shipping pork to the United States due to the U.S. countervail and U.S. inspection harassment at the border. This has meant that half of the plant's employees have lost their jobs. This affects much more than Moose Jaw. Intercontinental Packers of Saskatoon have cut their shipments of hogs to the U.S. from 5,000 a week to 1,500 and are contemplating ceasing shipments altogether.
In fact, in 1988, 53 per cent of hog exports were to the U.S. and represented some $410 million in trade. These trade dollars are now in jeopardy. Not only are Canadian producers and processors upset, but Clover Dale Meats of Minet, North Dakota have stated that they prefer Canadian hogs to American hogs.
February 9, 1990

This government said that the free trade agreement would be good for Canada, yet Moose Jaw Packers is forced to search for markets 1,200 miles away in Vancouver and 2,000 miles away in Ontario, instead of 400 miles south in Minet, North Dakota in a market that wants Canadian pork.
There is nothing free in this free trade agreement for Canadians. It is time to tear up this agreement right now.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the small business community continues to be a vital component of our national economy. Statistics show that between 1978 and 1987 over 1.5 million net new jobs were created across Canada through small, independent business ventures.
These Canadian small businessmen and women continue to demonstrate that initiative. Coupled with sound planning and a lot of hard work, they can be successful and prosperous all across our country.
I cite Dollard Landry's company, Atlantic Mini Bar Inc., which is a new and thriving business in Moncton, New Brunswick as a prime example.
Small business, without hesitation, continues to be the backbone of our economy. It is one of the greatest sources of new ideas, opportunities, wealth and employment. Like all members, I wish to pay tribute to the men and women across Canada who have and will embrace the bold Canadian spirit of small business entrepreneu-rialism.

Mr. Speaker, Dr. Leslie Harris, in his recent report on the Atlantic fisheries crisis, stated that commercial extinction occurs when it is no longer profitable to go after fish. We think we are fast approaching this point.
No one has accurate figures, but the federal Department of Fisheries estimates that the harp seal population
has grown from 2 million to about 3 million in the past six years. Estimates of how much these seals eat, whether it is herring, capelin, cod, crab or other commercial fish, is placed between 3 million and 10 million tonnes a year. It is estimated that 90 per cent of the fish they consume are commercially important.
No matter how you do the mathematics, it is apparent that seals catch between two and seven times as many fish each year as the entire Canadian fishing fleet and it costs the fishery close to $90 million a year.
I join many others in publicly calling on the Government of Canada to implement now, immediately, a cull of the seal herd population using appropriately sized vessels and using idle plant capacity to process the seal meat. This in itself is not enough. To complement this, the government should initiate an aggressive public relations campaign aimed at countering any future boycotts of Canadian products at home and abroad resulting from the seal management issue.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Science and Technology)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to draw to the attention of the House the support of the English community of the Quebec metropolitan area for the Meech Lake Accord.
By a resolution passed on Monday, January 29, the association Voice of English Quebec stated that it was in favour of supporting the Meech Lake Accord.
Voice of English Quebec stated also that the accord brings the province of Quebec fully into the constitutional family and urges the First Ministers, the Government of Canada and the provinces to take all necessary steps to ensure the passage of the Meech Lake Accord and to commit themselves formally to a process for further constitutional renewal.
The support of this important group from Quebec for the Meech Lake Accord proves once more that the accord must be ratified as is, without delay, in the best interests of all Canadians.

February 9, 1990

Mr. Speaker, the Department of External Affairs has told Radio Canada International to disband its German broadcasting system in favour of switching to Arabic.
Events have changed radically in Europe. It means that that has become a poorly timed decision, to say the least. It is important to note that the German service is not only broadcast on shortwave, the service is also picked up between 6.30 and 7 p.m. daily on a local Berlin FM station. This enables us to present a Canadian perspective to the people of Berlin. It comes out of an old post-war arrangement the allies made. We do this through the British Broadcasting corporation. This is really something that we have. At a time when there is talk of German reunification, this access to people in East and West Germany should not be abandoned.
We have a large German-Canadian community that is interested in this as well. I have written to the Secretary of State for External Affairs about this decision, asking him to reinstate the German service of Radio Canada International.
At this time in Europe, with the momentous events that are happening and with our access, we should not give that up.

Mr. Speaker, a few days ago a member opposite stated that a car dealer in his riding was concerned about how the GST would affect his business. He clearly does not understand that the principle of GST is to completely relieve Canadian business of the federal sales tax burden.
As a new car dealer for 15 years, I see very tangible positives for dealers in several ways. First, inventories. Dealers carry large volumes of inventory. The GST will reduce the dollar amount and the cost of carrying that inventory.
Second, operating costs. Any business that consumes materials, tools, supplies and facilities, will see their costs of operation go down.
Third, and probably most important, the benefits to purchasers. All customers will see the after-tax price of vehicles go down.
In particular, farmers, fishermen and commercial customers in the system will benefit even more because they are relieved completely of both the FST and the GST, about a $2,000 reduction on a $20,000 pick-up.
As well as the positives, of course, there are always some negatives, mostly relating to transitional issues. These are now being addressed by the Department of Finance. By any standards, the positives of GST far outweigh the negatives in this business as in other small businesses.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
In
June 1988, the Conservative Government announced it would establish a Postal Services Review Board that would be responsible for examining changes in postal rates and postal services and submitting recommendations to the government.
Last Tuesday, however, when the chairman of the relevant committee appeared before the House committee, he told us that so far, his committee's experience and the consultation process had been disappointing. He added that after a full year of operating as an advisory body, the Postal Services Review Committee felt that if the review process did not improve substantially during the current year, the government should consider amending the proposed status of the Postal Services Review Board and making it a regulatory body.
On behalf of the Official Opposition, I invite the responsible minister to table forthwith a bill that confers real powers on the Postal Services Review Board, so that it can discharge its responsibilities and prevent the Canada Post Corporation from raising rates and reducing service.
February 9, 1990

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we know that when democratic rights and privileges are widely abused, anarchy will result.
We also know that when lawmakers circumvent then-own rules, they promote the very disorder the rules were intended to prevent. The planned and deliberate actions of the New Democratic Party to thwart the rules and orders of the House in pursuit of their own ends is exactly the kind of conduct that creates disorder and breeds anarchy.
Do hon. members want examples? The member for Nickel Belt went to a flea market in Nova Scotia to gather anti-GST petitions in defiance of the ancient rule of parliamentary petition.
The NDP House leader announced on TV his intention to stall and delaiy House business. This is conduct contemptuous of the parliamentary process. No wonder The Ottawa Citizen warns the NDP not to stall Parliament and states: "Play by the rules, not with the rules. All Canada is watching".

Mr. Speaker, there is an illness that is affecting one in a hundred Canadians but that no one seems to want to talk about. That illness is schizophrenia, a disease which costs Canadians over $3 billion in direct health care and support costs each year. This brain disease often leads to hallucinations, thought disorders, loss of emotions and an inability to function in a work environment.
Federal funding for schizophrenia research is only $2 million per year. The quality of research is excellent and research results have greatly improved the outlook for discovering the causes and methods for preventing and curing this terrible brain disease. More needs to be done. Including private funding, cancer research in Canada receives $300 per patient, schizophrenia receives $17. The progress in combating schizophrenia is now just as possible as for cancer.
I urge the government on behalf of the thousands of Canadians afflicted by this disease and the families and friends who share their suffering to do more to help
Oral Questions
these physically able individuals to become fully productive members of our society.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the minister for employment. Today's statistics show that the unemployment rate has now increased for four consecutive months to 7.8 per cent, with over one million Canadians unemployed and major plants closing all over this country.
In these circumstances, I ask the minister when the government will change its hands-off policy to counteract this disturbing trend in the economy, to change its policy to stimulate economic growth and save these jobs, or are the government and the minister willing to accept the 8.5 per cent unemployment rate predicted in the Minister of Finance's budget last April? Is the government going to put its head in the sand and let thousands of jobs go down the drain in this country?

Mr. Speaker, I suggest to the hon. member that for the month of January, he should read the statistics for what they are. The number of new jobs increased by 42,000. The reason why there was a marginal increase in unemployment was that the number of people working increased. I think the performance is good. I would put our record of job creation against that of the former Liberal government any time.

Mr. Speaker, we are not talking about a marginal increase in unemployment. We are talking about a four month trend in which unemployment has increased substantially. I remind the minister that in 1981-1982, which he and the Prime Minister often refer to, the western world was in a recession. The Liberal government did something about it and changed that situation around, which was evident in 1984.
This government is willing to tolerate high interest rates, a declining trade situation, high employment and at the same time is bringing in new taxes which economists say will accelerate the recession. How can the minister justify this blend of policies at this time as we

February 9, 1990
Oral Questions
face a recession? How can he justify that trend? How can he be so callous toward the unemployed in this country?

Mr. Speaker, this government recognizes that lower rates of interest would be good for the economy. That is why it supports the Bank of Canada in its policy to bring interest rates down in a way that will allow them to stay down. We cannot work on this artificially. We support the Bank of Canada's approach to fight inflation. Inflation is the threat. If we did not act in this way, we would not be acting responsibly. Again, without any hesitation, I would put our record on this side of the House against that of the former Liberal government.

Mr. Speaker, since 1984 the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance have claimed credit for every job created in this country as if the private sector and the international market-place had nothing to do with it. They had all the answers. That was easy in an expanding economy, but the real test of a government's policies is in a declining economy. If they have the answers to these problems, I ask the minister to show them to us today, and reverse this four-month trend of unemployment. What is the minister going to do about it? What new policies is he going to give the Canadian people?

Mr. Speaker, I think we are doing exactly what needs to be done. We are taking very tough decisions. GST is one of them. The terrible tax on the Canadian economy, the 64-year old manufacturers' sales tax which destroys jobs, is being removed. For 50 years groups have said that Canada must change this system. We are doing it. We are making sure that inflation does not run away like it did in the early 1980s when interest rates were above 20 per cent and inflation rates above 10 per cent.

Mr. Speaker, this question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. This morning the minister confirmed
fears anticipated by the youth of our nation. At a time when they are faced with higher tuition fees, escalating education costs, an unbearable debt load and devastating double digit unemployment, the minister in her wisdom decided to respond to this already grave situation by cutting the seed program by 35 per cent and wrongfully denying summer job opportunities for young Canadians. How can the minister justify this action?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Youth)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very proud of the initiative that we announced today. It is a stay-in-school initiative. As the hon. member knows, people who are on our social welfare system and back on UI are very often people with a grade 10 education. If we can convince them to stay in school until they are in grade 12, their chances of better employment are doubled. We think it is very important that our young people, looking at the future for them and the kind of lives they can lead, stay in school. That is the first point.
The second point is that last summer in many areas there were more jobs than there were students to fill them. What we have tried to do is look at an area of greater need. There will be a regional balance to the summer employment program so that we continue to be sensitive to the needs of students where employment conditions are not so good.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same minister, whose rhetoric is quite unacceptable. Not only is the minister's policy direction misguided, but it steals money and opportunities away from post-secondary education students to pay for high school drop-outs. How can the minister pit two needy groups of our society, the post-secondary education student and the high school drop-out against each other? How can she morally justify that? Does she not know that both need our help?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Youth)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would certainly like to remind the hon. member of how we feel with regard to our young people that the youth unemployment rate in 1984, when his party was in power, was 18.2 per cent. The youth unemployment rate now is 12 per cent. That
February 9, 1990

means that young people and students are considerably better off today than they were then.
I would also point out that there are a greater number of high school students in need across this country than there are at the post-secondary level. The hon. member should be congratulating us. If we cannot keep people in school, they are not going to achieve the post-secondary level. It is very important that those young people be encouraged to stay in school.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to he or she who will answer today for the Minister of Finance. Yesterday the interest rates hit a five-year high. The Conference Board has observed that the economy is in the same state as it was in 1981. In Windsor the focus of the automobile industry in Ontario, accountable for 140,000 direct jobs and responsible as the engine of growth for the economy over the period of the last seven years, the unemployment rate has hit 13 per cent, chiefly because of lay-offs in the automobile industry. That was the first fiscal sign in 1981 of the downturn that followed. My question to whoever is speaking for the Minister of Finance is this: Is this really the time to be talking about a tough budget that is going to cause yet more unemployment and economic troubles in this country?
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I remind the hon. member that there are no miracle policies. There are difficult decisions to steer the economy on a good course. This is the course we are following.
We want to be sure that inflation does not run away from us. This would be devastating for members of the hon. member's riding and for all Canadians. We know that we need to bring interest rates down. We must do that by fighting inflation, by making sure that we can bring them down.
In mid January we saw the first sign that things were easing up a bit. The pressures in the economy which cause these rates were diminishing. We brought the rate down to some extent, but it is a very volatile situation. We need to manage it in the best interest of Canadians.
Oral Questions
In the meantime, I think our policies are the only good policies that can be followed. Over the years they have resulted in a a very good performance compared to any other industrial country.

Mr. Speaker, it is perfectly clear that everybody knows that the interest rate policy is not in the best interests of anybody. It is not in the best interests for the Minister of Finance to be communicating that there is going to be a tough budget that is going to affect the middle class and the poor and the regions yet more. In the province of Quebec the unemployment rate has gone from 9.5 to 10.5 per cent. This is one of the regions that will be most affected by Bill C-21.
I ask the minister whether it is not time to withdraw Bill C-21 as a part of a whole series of actions that ought to be taken to address the fact that we face not inflation, but high unemployment rates because of an economic downturn that will affect a great many people in this country.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Youth)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I have said in this House before, Bill C-21 is designed precisely to help those who are the first hit in an economic downturn. Those who need training are thrown into unemployment quickly. The workers we have spoken to and the surveys we have conducted among unemployed workers indicate that the reason they cannot get jobs is they do not have the skills.
Our job as a government is to make sure that they do have the skills. That is why we need Bill C-21 and need it quickly. That is why we have the stay-in-school initiative that I announced this morning, so that young people in Canada will have the right high school education in order to have job training for the future. We are focusing on regional development because job training and regional development go together. That is what this government has done. It has taken tough decisions on those things and they are the right ones.

Mr. Speaker, the government is adopting policies that are going to increase the unemployment rate. It has a bill that will lengthen the qualifying period and shorten the payment period. Then the minister has the nerve to talk about the stay-in-school initiative. The Challenge program is being cannibalized to introduce a half-baked program that the minister could not even describe in

February 9, 1990
Oral Questions
detail this morning. Is that the answer to the unemployment situation we face in the future? That is outrageous.
I ask the government again to reconsider this cocka-mamie, bucket of programs that have no relationship to the realities of this country. In the portions of this country on which this economy depends, the unemployment rates are going up. I ask the government to lower the interest rate policy, to do something about changing the budget direction. It is going to be hurtful. Increase the government's role in helping those who will be affected.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Youth)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure there was some kind of question in there. I want to correct the impression about the stay-in-school initiative that was announced today. I am sure if the hon. member has done his homework, he knows that federal labour market programs and services now directed at in-school youth are going to be increased. Those are programs that are working. They include co-op education, work orientation workshops, Canada Career Week and counselling services.
In addition, within my own department the job entry programs under Canadian Jobs Strategy are directed at our young people as well. We spend within our own framework alone $700 million on the young people of this country.
That is money well spent. We know that they will be better educated. They will be better trained, and they will have much better and more stable futures with the kinds of programs we are providing than with the kind of crap the NDP talks about.

Mr. Speaker, given the paucity of senior ministers over there, I will direct my question to whom it may concern. I want to raise the serious issue involving the chairman of the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture.
John Kim Bell, the first native Canadian to become a symphony orchestra conductor, has said that the chairman of the Communications and Culture Committee has called native Canadians lazy. This is a very serious matter and something which cannot be ignored.
I am aware of the fact that the hon. member has already denied making the statement. He has said that the statement is inaccurate.
However, the government cannot escape its responsibility. I want to know where the government stands on this issue and whether the government accepts the member's statement.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, sooner of later perhaps the hon. member will recognize that his responsibilities as a member of Parliament require a little more discipline and attention to detail than simply being a talking head on television.
He will know that the member in question took the first opportunity today to rise in the House of Commons to make an apology and, among other things, to say on the record of the House of Commons that he did not make the statements attributed to him.
The hon. member will know, if he knows anything about Parliament, that there is an elemental rule here which says that the word of a member is accepted. That finishes the matter.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, if the minister was listening closely, he would have heard me quote the hon. member saying that he denied making the statement and that the statement was inaccurate. I quoted the hon. member, and I am not going to take any lessons from the senior minister.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext: You should.
My supplementary questions is this-
Oh, oh!

Perhaps the jackals would just shut their mouths for a moment.
I think there is a lesson for all of us. I think there is much too much loose talk in this country-
We are hearing some of it right now.

-and I think it is incumbent upon all of
us to get a grip on ourselves.

The chairman was elected on the strength of the majority of the Conservatives on the committee, obviously on the recommendation of the government. Despite the hon. member's denial, does the government still support the chairman in that role as chairman of the committee?
When will the government stop the hon. member from always putting his foot in his mouth?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The first part of the question is out of order. There were two parts to it, and the right hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs may answer the second part.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member believes that there is too much loose talk in the country, I can suggest a direct contribution he might make to solving the problem.
There is a rule in the House with respect to accepting the word of the member. The member has given his word and it therefore must be accepted.
Therefore, the government does not intend to act on an allegation which has been denied following the proper procedures in the House. This government, as a product of the House of Commons, intends to respect the rules and traditions of the House of Commons.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to get back to the Minister of State (Finance) and ask him this: If the current sales tax is so bad for employment, why did the government increase this tax four times in the last four years? And since in the past, the government took the credit when unemployment rates went down, why does the same government refuse to take the responsibility for the present increases in the unemployment rate? Why is it so indifferent to the people of this country?

Mr. Speaker, this government is certainly not indifferent to the circumstances of Canadians and Canadian workers.
Oral Questions
In fact, we have had policies that were central to the economic development of this country. I am not going to claim that all the good things that happened in Canada were a direct result of the government's actions, but they would certainly not have occurred if the environment had not been favourable.
We increased the existing tax because it is one of the pillars of our system for raising revenue, a pillar that has its faults and has been around for 64 years. However, when we saw the impact it had on a country that must become increasingly competitive, we decided, considering our general development strategy which included the Free Trade Agreement and other measures, to introduce this tax reform which is not very popular but necessary, difficult, but good for the country.
Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there are some serious contradictions in its policy when the government admits that the present sales tax is one of the pillars of its economic policy and at the same time is saying that it is a silent killer of jobs in this country. My supplementary for the Minister of Employment and Immigration is as follows: If the government is not indifferent to Canadians, why will it cut the student summer employment program this summer and what is the government going to do for those students who used the program last summer? What is the government going to do for this important group?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Youth)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I pointed out in my earlier answer, the program will remain regionally sensitive in areas where there is higher unemployment among students.
In the meantime, in parts of southwestern Ontario, not all of it-and we have gone through this very carefully-there are certainly places where there were more jobs than there were students to fill them.
We believe it is a higher priority for the country, and I think the public would agree with us, to ensure that high school students remain in school in order that they can then qualify to be in the post-secondary stream about which the hon. member is so worried.
Oral Questions STATUS OF WOMEN

February 9, 1990

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the minister responsible for the status of women in Canada.
All through Canadian society we see negative attitudes and sexism rampant toward women. Last night, Supreme Court of Canada Justice Bertha Wilson said that "some aspects of criminal law in particular cry out for change since they are based on presuppositions about the nature of women and women's sexuality which in this day and age are a little short of ludicrous".
She cited studies that show sexism is the underlying premise in many judgments and that gender based myths, biases and stereotypes are deeply embedded in the attitudes of many male judges.
Will the minister consult with the Minister of Justice? Will she make input into the inner cabinet of this government and insist on training programs for judges? Will she insist that the Minister of Justice work with the provinces to ensure that judges receive education and training in women's equality issues, in sexual assault issues against women and wife battering? Will the minister do that?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Youth)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can assure the hon. member that this is something I regard as an ongoing part of my job. I have been doing it from the beginning.
I point out to the hon. member that probably she and I are in some agreement on the subject. We understand the references Justice Bertha Wilson made. We all have to work toward making some of those changes.
Since we have been in office this government has not only agreed that women, for example, should be better represented in the judiciary, but we are working very hard to achieve that.
We have made a total of 222 new appointments to the bench and elevated 66 judges to higher judicial office throughout the land. Of the new appointments, 37 have been women or 16.7 per cent of the total. Clearly we would like to improve on that, but it is a fairly good record so far. More significant, 16 of the 66 judges
elevated to higher office or 24 per cent have been women.
In addition, we are following with interest the judicial education centre which, in its early formulative stages, the government was helping to promote and encourage with the judiciary in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the slight progress in appointing women judges and women into positions of authority, but it is very slight. The record speaks for itself.
A judge in Quebec has said: "Rules are like women. They are meant to be violated". A judge in the Northwest Territories said sexual assault was not as serious there because "women get drunk and men see a pair of hips and help themselves". A judge in B.C. blamed a three-year old girl, a child, and called her sexually aggressive. She in fact was seen as responsible for her own assault. A judge in Nova Scotia was removed from the bench for telling women that they should obey their husbands and go back to them.
It is just not good enough. The time for action is now. It is past time for real action.
Will the minister consult with the Minister of Justice? Will we see real action for mandatory training programs for judges on the issues of women: women's sexuality and equality for women in the judicial system?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Youth)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have already said that I regard this issue as an important part of my job.
I think it also goes back much further than that. The audience whom Justice Bertha Wilson was addressing on this topic was a very important audience because these things start in law school. They probably start in high school. They do not all of a sudden spring into place when people are on the bench. I am sure the hon. member would agree with that, as would the Minister of Justice.
In the meantime, we are making better progress than has been made in the past; not as good a progress as I would like to see us make in the future or that this government, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice would like to see us make.
February 9, 1990

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Revenue.
The people of Red Deer, and I am sure all thinking Canadians, are becoming increasingly concerned about the need for deficit reduction and spending restraint. They are rightfully concerned about a report suggesting that the government will need an army of bureaucrats to administer the proposed goods and services tax.
In a time of restraint and given the Canadian taxpayers' desire to see a stronger effort in reduced spending and tax fairness, why do 3,000 or 4,000 tax police and collectors have to be hired to administer the proposed goods and services tax?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows, this government has continued to reduce government spending five years in a row, to the point of reducing the deficit by $10 billion.
$10 billion, that is not out of the Department of Finance.

In so far as people required to administer the GST is concerned, late last year I predicted a maximum number required of 3,900 people, and that was before discussions progressed with the provinces-and I am pleased to announce that those discussions are progressing very well-in order to eliminate any overlaps or duplications.
Let me make one thing clear, Mr. Speaker: there are no tax police. Of the total amount of people required to administer and prepare for a smooth launch of the GST, only 11 per cent of those people will be tax collectors. The rest are there to plan, to reach out to the business community, to provide technical and information assistance, and to prepare and plan GST credits for low and modest income Canadians and senior citizens. Those are not tax policemen. They are people to process payments, claims and refunds to businesses and to assist the small business community to plan in an orderly, smooth, efficient and simple fashion.
That is what this is. It is a service. Once and for all let us put it to rest: there are no tax police.
