speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to table an Order in Council confirming the intention of the Government of Canada to participate fully in the United Nations observer group in Central America.
As I announced on November 30, 1989, in concert with the Secretary of State for External Affairs, Canada has dispatched nine officers to Honduras as part of the UN's advance party. I am pleased to announce that a further 12 observers are being deployed.
As well, the first elements of an approximately 100-person helicopter squadron was deployed beginning this week. It will continue to be deployed during the month of February to Central America where it will join the UN observer group known by its Spanish acronym of ONUCA.
I would like to emphasize that Canada's involvement in the Central American peace process should not be seen as something new, but something that has been evident for a number of years, especially over the last decade. My colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and others in this House have visited the region a number of times and those visitations were to promote the peace process.
Following the August, 1987, signing of the Esquipulas II Agreement in Guatemala City, an agreement that outlined, "a procedure for the establishment of a firm and lasting peace in Central America", this House
created a Special Committee on the Peace Process in Central America to consider Canada's participation in the peace process.
An important recommendation of that committee stated: "If and when a verification force of some kind is created and Canada is requested by the five to participate in the force, then Canada should favourably consider such a request". Today, I am able to say that we have been able to comply with the recommendations of that special committee.
You will also recall, Mr. Speaker, that when it became obvious that the peace process would require a verification mechanism, the five Central American nations turned to Canada, Spain and the Federal Republic of Germany to undertake this mission. It was Canada which, while giving full support to the peace plan, pushed to have the United Nations intimately involved in the process. We can now take some degree of credit for seeing this phase of the peace plan being conducted under the auspices of the United Nations.
We have supported UN involvement, as did the special committee on Central America, because we believe that it is the most credible and competent authority to undertake peacekeeping operations. This belief is firmly tied to our support for the obvious capacity of the United Nations for peacemaking.
You may well ask this question, Mr. Speaker. Why deploy a UN observer mission now? If one looks carefully at the situation in the region, one quickly arrives at the conclusion that there will never be a perfect time to deploy a UN observer group.
In November, we applauded the Secretary General's initiative to deploy an advance party to Honduras as a potential catalyst to re-establish the political consensus in the region and as a means of stabilizing the situation there.
At that time we also indicated that we expected to continue to participate in the UN decision-making process throughout the subsequent phase-by-phase deployment into the Central American countries. Obviously, we have closely monitored the situation and we are prepared to commit both military observers and a helicopter unit of the Canadian Forces in this next phase.
For those who are concerned about the risks involved to our peacekeepers, let me remind you of what was said in the Bosley report: "The risks of involvement in Central America are considerable, but the risks of non-involvement or turning a blind eye to a genuine
February 9, 1990

appeal from the five, would be a failure of responsibility and of self-interest on Canada's part."
As I stated earlier, there is no perfect moment in which to deploy our peacekeepers and there are inherent risks in peacekeeping at any time. But in the case of Central America the level of risk is manageable and is justified by the importance we attach to the process of advancing peace in that region. If at any time we conclude that these risks are becoming unacceptable we will, obviously, reconsider the total situation and our role in it.
As our peacekeepers are certainly aware, they are continuing a long and proud tradition of members of the Canadian Forces in the name of peace throughout the world.
The steps toward peace in Central America have been slow and at times painful. But progress is being made, and progress will continue to be made.
The dispatch of our peackeeping forces to another region is a sign of Canada's willingness to help those who seek peace and security anywhere in the world.
I know that you, Mr. Speaker, will join with all members of the House in offering their best wishes and support to these Canadians who are serving the cause of peace and security around the world.

Mr. Speaker, we on this side obviously support this initiative. I do not have to tell the House or Canadians that it was the Hon. Lester Pearson who began the Canadian contribution, historic contribution, to peacekeeping with the Canadian peacekeeping force in Suez in 1956 which helped to resolve that crisis.
Indeed, Canada has a long and proud tradition in the world in peacekeeping, which this gesture now simply carries on.
However, I would say to the minister that I think Canada has to be careful in not sending mixed signals to the world. We find it ironic, for example, on this side that today we are sending a peacekeeping force to Central America and just recently we gave unconditional and unequivocal support to an armed invasion of Panama.
Routine Proceedings
Canada should not be for peace at one moment and war at the next. I think that that kind of signal strains Canada's credibility and does not do anything to enhance our reputation. We believe that Canada has to be careful in the kind of signal it sends to Central America. We believe that Canadians were disappointed with the government's support of the American invasion of Panama.
I would further say to the Minister that we also believe that while the monitoring of the situation in Central America is important, that perhaps considering the conflicts in places like El Salvador, for example, the mandate of the mission might be expanded and that that might be helpful.
There is another thing that I want to suggest to the minister, that we simply go further than the sending of missions. Perhaps there is a role for Canada in an expanded peacekeeping operation.
I want to remind him that we on this side, particularly the member for Eglinton-Lawrence and our members from Prince Edward Island, suggested to the government that perhaps Summerside become a base for the training of peacekeepers and for peacekeeping operations. We were disappointed the government did not support that suggestion. I put it forward again and ask the minister if he would reconsider on behalf of the people of Summer-side, and the people who serve there, Canada's expanded role in peacekeeping.
I would further point out to the minister that in the last budget new communications equipment for our soldiers was discontinued. If our forces are going to Central America and other places in the world, they need to be as well equipped as we can make them. I further ask the minister to reconsider the cancellation of the new communications equipment for our soldiers.
Basically, we in this party, as I am sure all Canadians, support this initiative by the government. We believe that is is an important contribution, a contribution that Canada should make.
I want to join with the minister in wishing our Canadian forces who go to Central America all good wishes for themselves and for a speedy recovery of the situation there.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond on behalf of the New Democratic Party to the minister's statement. Let me begin by saying that we join with the rest of the House in support of the Canadian forces personnel going to Central America

February 9, 1990
Routine Proceedings
who are making their contribution on behalf of Canada to the peace process there.
I might also say as an aside that coming from Winnipeg I am aware with respect to another peacekeeping operation that the PPCLI, the Princess Patricia Canadian Light Infantry, are about to embark on their third tour, I believe, of Cyprus. There will be a ceremony to mark that in Winnipeg next Tuesday, a ceremony which I am unable to make. That is why I want to mention it today. It points out one of the dangers of peacekeeping, namely, there are some situations in which we have been peacekeeping now for 25 years. We hope that will not be the case in Central America. We hope this will be part of a process that will reach some kind of happy conclusion in a much shorter time period than has been the case in Cyprus.
As the minister stated today, this most recent United Nations peace monitoring effort is not the beginning of Canadian efforts to bring peace to Central America. Members of Parliament, church workers, NGOs, and a great variety of Canadians have been involved over the years from all walks of life in Central America.
The government has chosen the course of promoting multilateralism with respect to solving the problem in Central America, in this case through the United Nations. We are all hopeful that approach will succeed.
As the hon. member for Labrador pointed out, there is an inconsistency in the extent to which the government promotes multilateralism on the one hand and yet when confronted with unilateral action, as it was in the case of the American invasion of Panama, it remained silent-in fact, it does not remain silent but approves of a unilateral action.
If you want to be wholly, shall we say, in favour of multilateralism, then one has to be consistent and be critical of unilateral actions when they appear as they did in the case of the American invasion of Panama. Yet the government took the wrong position on that.
It is a position which I think was implicitly, if not explicitly, criticized in the recent report of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade where it stated with regard to Canada's membership in
the OAS that we had to get beyond this sort of unilateral action-the United States acting as a policeman according to its own ethics in Central America.
We should not take all that much comfort in this particular announcement. It is an important step along the road to peace, but there are many steps yet to be taken.
Indeed, appearing before the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade in December, the director of the Peacekeeping Operations Directorate, Colonel Don Ethell, pointed out that the ONUCA operation in Central America was a unique exercise in many ways.
I might say that I have had the opportunity to know Colonel Ethell and to travel with him in Central America when I was part of the Special Committee on the Peace Process in Central America. I would like to take this opportunity to compliment him on the work that he has done. He is certainly a very professional man and someone in whom we can all take a great deal of pride in his peacekeeping work.
ONUCA will be proceeding within the context of an agreement concluded between the five countries in the region which are not in direct conflict with each other. Colonel Ethell pointed out what he and the rest of the committee were all too aware of. The root of instability in Central America is not country-to-country fighting, it is civil unrest. It is what is happening within the countries.
The ONUCA team is not there to act as a negotiator. It is not there to act as a police force. Indeed, Colonel Ethell stated that the UN peacekeeping forces or observer missions are there to provide a UN presence, an international presence. They are there to provide stability so that the politicians and the diplomats can cany on with the peace process. They are not there to solve the political problems.
With your indulgence, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say just a word or two on the political problem. This whole announcement begs the question: What is the government doing about the political problem?
February 9, 1990

Has this government approached the Bush administration and voiced the concerns of many Canadians about U.S. support for the Contras in Nicaragua? Has the government questioned the $1.4 million a day in military assistance to the ARENA government in El Salvador? Perhaps now that Canada will have a military presence in Central America through ONUCA the government will follow on this initiative and press the United States to stop interfering in the sovereignty of Nicaragua and El Salvador.
The United States has done everything in its power short of invasion to disrupt and discredit the election process in Nicaragua, for instance. I wonder what the reaction would be in Washington if this government, or any government, openly provided $9 million to the Democrats in an election year, as the U.S. has done for the anti-Sandinista coalition in Nicaragua.
In El Salvador, the recent FMLN offensive has proven that despite massive U.S. support of Salvadoran armed forces there will be no military solution to the decade old civil war. There has to be a political solution. Crucial to that political solution are the actions and the intent of the United States of America, and that is where Canada comes in. That is where we have a role as a friend of America to say: "You need to be playing your part in this peace process, and that means stop funding those who have no intention of having a political solution".
We welcome the announcement. We all wish our peacekeeping forces well. It is going to be a dangerous job. Helicoptering around Central America is not exactly something that I would wish on anybody. But that is what people in the Armed Forces are for. They know that when they go in. We commend them for their responsibilities in that area. We hope that they all return safely in a context that sees progress toward peace in Central America.
['Agreed.']

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry Weiner (Secretary of State of Canada and Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a lot of people in Canada today have found a new lease on life. They are finally shedding a cloak of secrecy they have worn for years at school, work and home. These people face the future with a mixture of fear and optimism as they summon the courage to stand up and say, "No, I cannot read or write".
Routine Proceedings
Our fellow Canadians who lack literacy skills will be helped this year with more commitment and compassion than ever before. All around the world 1990 is being observed as International Literacy Year.

It is a year declared by the United Nations as a time for self-awareness, study, hard work, understanding, patience, and above all-hope.
For its part, the government of Canada has made a long-term commitment to the cause of literacy. Through the national literacy program, we have already given support to develop more than 400 literacy projets and activities in partnership with community organizations, volunteer associations, business and labour.
We also have agreements with every provincial and territorial government covering joint initiatives to promote literacy. Ours is clearly a cooperative approach to a major social challenge.

These innovative projects include the development of literacy materials, setting up learners' conferences, studying ways in which training may be made more accessible and promoting literacy in the workplace.
As well, other government departments have become closely involved in the literacy movement. For example, the Solicitor General supports a program which gives inmates the opportunity to complete an adult basic education program before their release.
The Canadian International Development Agency includes literacy as a key component in the success of its development programs.
The Canada Employment and Immigration Commission sponsors literacy efforts directed at enhancing the employability of workers and youth. Of course, these are only a few examples among others.
Canada's future economic competitiveness and social development will depend on the existence of a highly skilled and adaptable workplace and workforce. Greater reading and writing skills are going to be called for in every area of national life from technology to the social sector.
The government has taken a leadership role in addressing the challenge of literacy, but we cannot do it alone.

February 9, 1990
Routine Proceedings

We need the willing partnership of all Canadians from every sector of society-during 1990, international literacy year, and for all the years to come.
Business and labour, parents and teachers, as well as volunteers-all have an invaluable contribution to making our country a nation of enthusiastic readers, young and old.

Literacy is key to the Canada of tomorrow. It is our guarantee of future success. I am confident that by working together Canadians will be able to make the dream of a more literate Canada come to life for our children and their children,

Mr. Speaker, the United Nations has proclaimed 1990 International Literacy Year.

This will be a time of increased awareness, study, hard work, understanding, patience and especially of hope.
The purpose of this proclamation, Mr. Speaker, is to make governments throughout the world aware of the need to address a matter that is important to us all.
The Secretary of State is to be commended for his speech, perhaps a bit brief but excellent nevertheless. I know the Secretary of State as a man of conscience and compassion, and I can only applaud those qualities.
During his speech, he mentioned that the Government of Canada had made a long-term commitment to literacy training. I may point out, Mr. Speaker,-

In September of 1988, the Mulroney government announced a $110 million grant for new literacy initiatives for the five years after 1988. I made a calculation and found that this works out to about $4 per year per student. I ask the government this. What kind of commitment is that?
Roughly, five million Canadians are functionally illiterate, unable to read, write, or compute at a level sufficient to let them participate fully in the Canadian
society. That is over 20 per cent of our population-one out of five Canadians.
The government's initiative is important, but is it enough? Will it continue past this year, the 1990 International Literacy Year, or are these just good words we have heard as a sort of short declaration?
The Canadian Business Task Force on Illiteracy has estimated that illiteracy costs Canadian business $4 billion a year and that the annual social cost of illiteracy could be as high as $10 billion.
I would like to refer to an article that appeared in this morning's The Globe and Mail. It states that Southam News in 1987 conducted a survey which discovered that Newfoundland alone, with its high rate of unemployment, faces further strain from layoffs in fish packaging plants. The survey revealed that 44 per cent of Newfoundland's adults were considered illiterate. That is quite a mouthful on the part of the Southam research. What will this government do to address this particular question?
I would like to finish by quoting-

-from a speech by the hon. member for Saint-Boniface (Mr. Duhamel) at the 42nd Convention of the Association canadienne d'education de langue frangaise, in Quebec City this summer. He said:
-that the general definition of illiteracy includes not only the illiterate as such but also the functionally illiterate.
He added:
-that illiteracy is not an isolated problem. It often occurs where there is poverty, hunger, excessive use of drugs and alcohol, violence and cultural alienation. To wipe out illiteracy, we also have to look at the following issues:	nutrition, child case and access to
transportation.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today on behalf of the New Democratic Party to respond to the minister on the issue of International Literacy Year. I would like to speak as directly as possible to the minister because I know he listens to these comments.
In 1987 the Southam literacy survey found that 4.5 million Canadians over the age of 18 were functionally
February 9, 1990

illiterate. More disturbing was the news that the number of illiterate Canadians is expected to continue to rise by 100,000 per year.
The Canadian government must make commitments to all those who are overcoming their fear, stepping forward and asking for help. This commitment must be a guarantee of access to literacy programs within our communities across the country. We must provide longterm funding to groups and organizations delivering those programs.
Learners must be able to find a program which fits their needs. Literacy organizations across Canada are attempting to provide such programs from the John Howard Society's literacy program, which the minister mentioned, to the Ontario Federation of Labour's workplace literacy scheme called BEST. These programs are off and running. We should celebrate that.
However, the programs face constant underfunding. There is no doubt that if this government made longterm financial commitments, these literacy groups and organizations could devote all their energies to battling this serious problem rather than raising funds. It is a good investment too. Business and community groups realize that the cost of illiteracy in the workplace is extremely high. It affects workers, productivity and morale. Furthermore, it is estimated that the cost to the Canadian economy is $10 billion a year.
We have to do other things and I remind members opposite that it is inconsistent to put a tax, the GST, on books at the same time as tackling illiteracy. There are some positive things the government could do. It could provide child care for single parents so they can participate in literacy programs. There is initiative. It could work with the actors who now have an illiteracy program whereby they go to suburban malls and hold celebrity readings. I hope they come to Coquitlam in my riding; it is a perfect place for it. I hope the minister will support that program.
In this International Year of Literacy, Canada still remains a long way from addressing the causes which lead to a great number of Canadians growing up unable to read. There still exists the vicious cycle of poverty which can lead to inadequate education, meagre job opportunities, and continued poverty in the next generation.
Routine Proceedings
On a personal note, I would like to tell the minister that I had a fellow in my office recently in Coquitlam, British Columbia, who used to be in the key business but is now unemployed. He confessed to me that he could not read and was going back to school. He has a family and he needs help to support the family when he goes back to school. But it was wonderful to talk to that person. That is part of what we are trying to convey. I say to the minister that we are all in this together. Let us be positive and work together as Canadians to tackle illiteracy this year so that we become the best educated workforce and population in the world because that is the key to industrial success.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too have a petition which I would like to table under the provisions of Standing Order 36.
This petition is signed by a number of Canadians who are upset with the GST, which stands for the goods and services tax, but which should stand for the grief and suffering tax. Those Canadians want tax reform and they also want the goods and services tax to be abolished, no matter what the rate.

Mr. Speaker, it is an honour and a privilege to present a petition on behalf of a number of my constituents from Deadman's Creek, Savona, Logan Lake, Lac Le Jeune, Cherry Creek and Red Lake.
These constituents are distressed that this government, in spite of the fact that 80 per cent of Canadians oppose this goods and services tax, continue to ram it through the Elouse of Commons. They point out that it is going to touch almost every aspect not only of their lives but of the lives of generations of Canadians to come. They feel that the government should listen to the people of Canada who are saying: "Do not proceed with this tax. Go back to the drawing board and essentially start all over."
They point out that this tax is unfair because it taxes all individuals, wealthy or poor, while our present tax system is biased in favour of the wealthy and the privileged. Mr. Speaker, I have two petitions signed by people from my former leader's constituency of Oshawa, as well as from surrounding communities of Ajax and Whitby.
These people, like millions of other Canadians, have recognized the government's goods and services tax for what it is, a tax grab on ordinary citizens which will drive up their cost of living and make an already unfair tax system even more unfair. Therefore, these people are
calling on us, as members of Parliament, to take seriously the democratic wish of the people of Canada, to send this tax back to the drawing board and come back with a tax system that will be fair to everybody and will not tax people who cannot afford to pay.

Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to stand, pursuant to Standing Order 36, to present a number of petitions in the House today.
The first petitions are, as a previous member has indicated, in opposition to the goods and services tax. These petitioners are from all over my riding, from the Marigold district, Saanich, the Ganges, Victoria. They are all opposed to this tax. What these petitioners want is real reform of the tax system.

Mr. Speaker, the second major petition that I have before the House today relates to another part of the world, the situation in El Salvador. There are nearly 500 signatures on this petition, once again from my riding.

ask that the government look again at that particular initiative.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to present a petition on behalf of a number of Canadians who are strongly opposed to the goods and services tax. This petition has been certified correct as to form and content.

They find it repugnant; they find it regressive, and they find it will be a terrible burden on them if it is introduced on Januaiy 1, 1991.
What those people were saying in Brandon this week and what these people who signed this petition are saying is that the government should wake up, listen to Canadians and stop this tax. Do not go ahead with it. They feel that if the government would just listen to Canadians, who have sound arguments and strong views and make a lot of sense about this tax, the government would come to its senses, and say, "No more. We are not going ahead with this tax. We are going to scrap it and we are going to go back to the drawing board".

Mr. Speaker, I believe I am also the next speaker. But I wanted to comment on some of the statements made by the hon. member for Port Moody- Coquitlam.
I was concerned when I heard some of the comments. I stand here now, not as the energy critic, which I am not, but as a member of Parliament from Newfoundland. His comments cause me great concern. I was surprised and very disappointed when I heard the position he was taking. I presume he was speaking for his party when he said that he was opposed to this bill going ahead for second reading.
Shame on you!

If that is not what the hon. member said, then that was the intent of the motion, although the motion has now been ruled out of order. I certainly got the opinion that there was less than enthusiastic support for this bill to go ahead.
I am very concerned about that for a number of reasons. I shall speak about the Hibernia project now. I recall very distinctly being in St. John's, Newfoundland. It was by accident that I was there on July 18, 1988, when the Prime Minister of this country came to Newfoundland. We had a very large and well-advertised meeting with the then Premier of Newfoundland, Brian Peckford, and there was great jubilation in Newfoundland.
The issue was, as much as these issues can be, non-political. Most and perhaps all Newfoundlanders rejoiced at the thought that there would be something around the comer other than the one industry that we have been working on for years and years-400 years plus.
I believe this is question and comment. I am going to ask you a question, but I had to lead up to the question. I have some time. I am also the next speaker, so you are going to have to hear a lot about this.
Government Orders
My concern is that on the principles espoused there was no concern for the number of jobs and opportunities that this will give Newfoundlanders, particularly at this time when the outlook is dismal. No matter how you look at the economy of Newfoundland, whether it is ACOA, regional funding, ERDAs, Bill C-21, funding for various projects, tourism, fishing, extension of the jurisdiction over the nose and tail of the bank, seal cull, whatever it is these days, the news is less than joyful. In fact, it is dismal. Hibernia has always been there as a hope, a ray of light at the end of the tunnel, at a time when, not only is the ray of light a bit dim but, in fact, you sometimes wonder whether there is a tunnel at all. I hear less than enthusiastic support from the hon. member. Yes, I am concerned and disappointed.
This project is not perfect; nothing in this world is perfect. I certainly strongly disagree and I am going to have to ask him precisely what he meant by the statement that fishing will always remain the one item that will keep Newfoundlanders alive. Surely we have to look at other things. We have to hold out some hope for the future, whether it is Hibernia or something else. Maybe tourism is a bit of a hope; we need to concern ourselves with this.
There was talk about feeding the beast. I am not sure which beast was being discussed but I was concerned that last June we ran into a problem with Hibernia simply because there was a problem with funding. We were looking at the plan by the consortia to build their so-called super modules and reduce the numbers from the 17 smaller ones for living quarters and production facilities atop the huge concrete base to five larger ones that would be differently structured.
I am concerned not just about the jobs of construction, which will be the initial jobs, the nuts and bolts of preparing the superstructure, but also about the follow-on jobs and whether there are 3,500 and 1,600. There is some debate over that right now. The fact of the matter is that these jobs are not nuts and bolts jobs, they are not mundane jobs, they are engineering skills, engineering skills in maintenance, in ballasting and reballasting, and these are the kind of skills that the Minister of Employment has been talking about and the things we are looking for.
I do not want to detract from some of the things I want to say later on, but I would like to ask the hon. member what precisely his concerns are with respect to why we

February 9, 1990
Government Orders
should not go ahead. Is he considering not only the immediate jobs that this is going to offer Newfoundlanders and, indeed, all Canadians since this is a Canadian project but also the advantages that are offered, not just by the jobs, but by the ray at the end of the tunnel, the morale boosting aspect of this? Does he not think that that outweighs all of the other concerns that he may have? I think it is also a question of risk analysis here and which of the two alternatives are the best or the least risky.

Mr. Speaker, we in the NDP are not against Hibernia. We are against this bill and we have made detailed comments against the bill, as I did in my speech.
As an outsider of Newfoundland-I come from the west coast of Canada-I am aware of and very sympathetic, as we all are, about the economic plight and the difficulties in Newfoundland. We want to hold out hope for Newfoundland but it should be real hope, should it not, and not false hope. We have seen in the past chocolate factories and cucumber factories. Successive Liberal and Conservative governments and politicians, in my view, have let the people of Newfoundland down with false hopes of pots of gold at the end of the rainbow. That is all I am saying, let us make sure it is real hope.
With respect, let me conclude with this. The ex-admiral said, "What about your criticisms of jobs"? Maybe we should go to the captain of the ship. We will go to Premier Clyde Wells. Here is what he said in interview with The Financial Post on October 2, 1989. He is a Liberal and the Premier of Newfoundland. The member said he is a good Liberal. That is right, he is a good Liberal. He said that the number of permanent jobs generated by this Hibernia project would be about the size of the workforce of two fish plants, and I quote:
The former government painted it as a saviour, it is not.
That was my position. What was the hon. member's position? He has taken a different position than Clyde Wells, the Liberal premier.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext: Order, please. Before I recognize the hon. member for Bonavista- Trinity-Conception, I wish to inform the House that because of ministerial statements, Government Orders will be extended by 34 minutes. Therefore, Private Members' hour will begin at 2.34 this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have the opportunity to comment on this bill. I was not going to go over any preliminaries, but in light of what I have heard this morning, I think it might be worth while to review for the members some of the things that have gone on with Hibernia, and perhaps to review some of the difficulties we have had in moving this project ahead.
I will start by commenting on the fact that we Newfoundlanders and most of us here in this House believed that the statement of principles that was signed on July 18, 1988, would go forward and indeed be approved on March 31 last year.
There was great disappointment that we ran into snags. This signature to the statement of principles was based on production going ahead in 1996. I understand that there has been a delay of at least one year. While that in itself is bad enough, we are concerned that at every turn, like on first reading, we had difficulties. In June 1989 we had concerns about the reduction in the number of modules that would be put on the gravity base structure and the consequent reduction of jobs.
Indeed, this is not a perfect set-up. It is not a perfect agreement. Certainly in the short time that I have been in the House I have not seen any perfect bill. This is why we go to committees and have the number of readings that we do.
I cannot impress upon this House the importance at this time in Newfoundland economic history for the Government of Canada, no matter which government is in power, to show that there is some concern and a will on the part of the Canadian government to do something that will assist eastern Canada, particularly Newfoundland.
The Hibernia oil field is located off the Grand Banks. For the information of the hon. member who talked about a couple of hundred miles, it is precisely 315 kilometres southeast of St. John's, Newfoundland. It is an elongated reservoir covering 20,000 acres. It has an estimated capacity of 525 billion barrels. The recovery of the oil will be through an offshore drilling rig that will have supports on the floor of the ocean with a platform above the water line.
February 9, 1990

This project is highly technical. I think it is safe to say it is on the cutting edge of technology. Some of the ideas are new. Some of them, if they cannot be considered revolutionary, are evolutionary in an uncertain sense. The plans have been refined at each turn of the clock. After a few turns of the clock, we ran into snags. That is to be expected.
I will accept the remarks attributed to the premier of Newfoundland, the Hon. Clyde Wells, that the jobs that would be engendered by this project would amount to the size of a couple of fish plants. As I said to the hon. member, a couple of fish plants would look pretty good right now. The fact of the matter is we have to start somewhere, even if there is a snag that comes up at every turn.
Yes, we are concerned about the environment, and yes we are concerned about toxic wastes. We are concerned about all these things, but in any project, any decision that I have had to make in recent life, nothing is clear-cut and dry. Everything is grey these days. You have to weigh the pros and the cons. Once I left school, one and one no longer equalled two. After leaving school, it is not quite one plus one equals two. It is sometimes three, and maybe 1.5.
This project has a tremendous future. It is a future that we have to concern ourselves with. This party supports this project for Canada, and especially Newfoundland.
There are some other principles that I received from our energy critic which I believe have direct application here.
The primary objective of our energy policy is to first and foremost gain the maximum economic benefit from the development of Canada's energy resources.
The second one is to ensure the security of Canada's energy supply. We are also concerned that we use energy in the most environmentally responsible way possible. Consistent with these three principles, we want to promote regional development consistent with economic reality.
It is estimated that oil from this project will be produced at 110 million barrels a day. It is not expected to flow until 1996-1997, depending on when the impediments to this bill are finally resolved and we get on with acting in a positive sense by approving the bill and giving it Royal Assent as soon as possible.
Government Orders
We are already a year behind the previous start-up schedule that was set in July 1988. It is imperative that we go ahead with this project as quickly as possible. It is expected to produce oil and there is no question that the oil is going to be higher priced. This is one of the great uncertainties. We can never say with any degree of confidence from month to month, even from week to week, what the price of oil is going to be. We all know that one wakes up in the morning without knowing what it is going to be. It is almost on a daily risk basis that we go forward with these projects.
There are some other down sides to this as well. There are some problems. I know that Premier Wells was speaking about his concern, one that I share, that perhaps we could have struck a better deal, that our royalties could have been increased and that maybe some of the tax concessions should not have been allowed. I do not want to get into that detail right now. I think those are the details we can get into after we examine it in committee and we look at some of the finer prints when we dot the i's and cross the r's.
The main concern we have now is with the statements of principles. We have to go forward with this now so that we can get into the detail. We can examine it in detail and make decisions and judgments amongst ourselves to come up with something that is reasonable. It probably will still be imperfect, but we are prepared to accept the imperfection of this kind of a deal.
We are dealing with the future. When you do not know for sure what the future is going to give you and what it is going to bring, you go on the best information you have at the time. The best information we have right now is that this is a worth-while project. It is a project that should go ahead and as soon as possible.
The statement of principles that has engendered a great deal of debate in this House engendered a great deal of debate in juxtaposition with some of the other principles that perhaps may be equally important in the future, but cannot be foreseen at this point in time. The statement of principles is something we have in front of us. We know what they are and we are dealing with them.
There are a number of statements of principle, but the one that I am going to concern myself about right now, in direct comparison to what the hon. member from Port Moody-Coquitlam had to say in his response, is the statement of principles calling for 3 million hours of employment to be created in Newfoundland during the four years of construction. Whether that is plus or minus

February 9, 1990
Government Orders
10 per cent, plus or minus 20 per cent, I am prepared to accept that as in the ballpark of what we are looking at.
The fact is that the oil companies changed the fundamental design and that complicates the situation. Anything that is changed invokes a complication and prevents them from carrying out this plan as had been previously agreed. The principles are not altered. Mr. Wells, the premier of Newfoundland, was quoted recently by The Globe and Mail in an article which I have as saying that the principles are not altered.
According to the article, he said: "We expect that they will ensure that there will take place in Newfoundland and in Canada as a whole work to the level that was agreed upon".
There are comments one might make here in the heat of of the battle or when anger sometimes flows, as is meant to happen in debate. Perhaps some statements one makes one regrets or would like to have said in a more positive sense. For all these statements, we have to look at this project in as positive a light as possible and I suggest, in as unpartisan a way as possible.
I on the one hand could not look at the negative aspects of this project attributed to the government and then, at the same time, stand on my feet and criticize the government for something that it is not doing.
This is an opportunity for the government to go forward with something that is potentially very helpful to Newfoundland and indeed to Canada. I would want my party to be seen as being very supportive of that initiative. Perhaps this is one of the rare times that we have gone forward in support of what the government plans to do. While we may have some difficulties with the technical details and with some of the wording of the statement of principles, I would be less than honest and forthright if I did not stand here and suggest that we move forward with it as soon as we can.
The economic benefit related to Newfoundland has to be considered beyond the millions of manhours that we talked about. Those benefits must also be considered in direct relationship with what the government claims to
be doing in the business of retraining people. I do not know what the bracket of the financing is going to be, and I do not think that has been actually worked out yet, but we know the gross figures. The project is going to cost $5.2 billion and there will be more money related to it later on. We know what the loan guarantees are and some of the most recent agreements.
Before I talk about the economic benefits in general, let me update the House about some of the most recent developments. Last June the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources was somewhat concerned-and we shared his concern-about precisely how the new agreement would come out and how it would affect the Statement of Principles with respect to the restructuring and reducing the number of modules from 17.
While it is safe to say that the machinery hit a snag I am delighted that, according to my information, we are back on track again. It is my understanding that the federal and the Newfoundland governments have agreed on a new joint proposal to the private sector consortium in an effort to get this energy development project back on track.
Apparently the federal energy minister was quoted as having said that no new money would come from Ottawa, but that some extra cash, as he called it, might become available from the Canada-Newfoundland Offshore Development Fund which, of course, has already been used. This is a $300 million account that was established in 1986, two years before the signing of the statement of principles, to help defray the cost of energy off the Newfoundland coast. About $235 million of that has already been earmarked of which $95 million was approved in 1988 as a part of this signing of this statement of principles for the Hibernia megaproject.
Apparently the $65 million left in the fund will be a factor in the upcoming negotiations with the oil consortia. Obviously this has to be part of the discussion. It is my understanding that Premier Wells has been meeting with the consortium members; that is Mobil Oil of Canada, Petro-Canada, Gulf Canada Resources and Chevron Canada Resources, all of Calgary, Perhaps we will hear more in the next two or three weeks on the specifics of the proposals.
February 9, 1990

Everybody has heard about the dismal situation that we now have in Atlantic Canada. I have two members with me now, the hon. member for Dartmouth and the hon. member for Malpeque. Everybody here has been aware of the crisis that we have had in Atlantic Canada.
We in Newfoundland-and I have to speak as a Newfoundlander now-do not like to have our hands out begging. Nobody likes to do that. We have had to resort to some pretty severe tactics in the last few years.
I remember growing up in Bonavista where my grandfather was a fisherman. I remember the meagre earnings of fishermen in those days. They lived simple lives, they lived happy lives, they ate healthy food and they had healthy habits. The situation, I regret to say some 45 or so years later, seems to have deteriorated from that of my memory.
I read a comment made by the commissioner of fisheries in Newfoundland about 100 years ago. The statements that he made 100 years ago are not too far removed from some of the statements that Dr. Harris made in his task force report on the fisheries. This is not meant as a criticism. These are facts and they cannot be disputed.
ACOA was reprofiled. Every week I get calls from disappointed people who perhaps are not aware of the rule changes. They believe that ACOA was meant to help them. They find stumbling blocks everywhere until they realize that there is not enough money there to launch their projects. I could cite 30 projects from one end of my riding to the other. I try to explain to these people that reprofiling means that there is less money. They understand but they are very disappointed.
There is less money for education and health. I am not going to harangue about the goods and services tax but it is not causing cheer in the hearts of men, women and children. Mr. Speaker, I know that you and I have had many discussions on Bill C-21, have sat in committee and listened to people. Whether you agree or disagree with the impact of the bill, the fact is there is a perception of what it will do to the unemployed in Newfoundland. Last year 79,000 people who drew unemployment insurance are going to be affected.
Government Orders
One study says that Newfoundlanders will lose the most. They will lose $2,540 on average. When you take out all the bipartisanship and all the things that perhaps are judgmental, the indisputable and relevant consideration is the morale of Atlantic Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, I know about morale and I know that you know about morale. Morale is very subjective. It is difficult to measure it, but you know what it is when you are among those whose morale is affected. You can walk on to a ship and within five minutes know whether the morale is high or low. How do you know? I cannot explain it. I went through my riding from one end to the other in mid-January for the specific purpose of talking to people and sensing their morale. It was not good.
Apart from the economic benefits, the statement of principles, the details, the complicated fundings, the royalties, the income tax and everything else, there is one ray of hope.
People talk to me and ask: "What is the hope? What is ahead?". I do not turn and criticize the government and say: "Well, this government does not know what it is doing". That is not good for morale and I do not say that. Not all of the time, Mr. Speaker.
I do say that tourism in perhaps 50 years will be good for Newfoundland. I say that it will get off the ground some day, perhaps not in my time. And we always look at Hibernia. If anybody in this House does anything to cripple the principles involved and the idea of Hibernia, this is going to be not just another little nail in the coffin of morale, but there will be no more hope. All hope will be diminished. It is in that context that I speak here as a member of the Opposition and as a Newfoundlander to ask members, when they are considering this very important bill, to bear that in mind in their consideration of the bill.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great interest to the comments of my hon. colleague and, as always, he has been very eloquent in his presentation and he has been very true to his constituency and exceptionally true to his province, the great province of Newfoundland.
I got a flavour of the importance of the Hibernia project to Newfoundlanders and to Atlantic Canada. I would hope that those on all sides of this House and those who are watching this debate did the same. In Atlantic Canada, all too often there are too few opportu-

February 9, 1990
Government Orders
nities to diversify. In Newfoundland in particular, where we have primarily resource-based industries in the fishery, we have seen the fishery go into a tailspin and a state of collapse.
Everybody likes to talk about diversification and prospects for a bright future. Hibernia has been a flicker of light at the end of a very dark tunnel for Newfoundlanders and Atlantic Canadians. There have been some worrisome delays in the past.
I am not here here today to blame or point a finger, but it worries me considerably that we have waited as long as we have to get the Hibernia project under way. It worries me considerably that at some point there was discussion about altering the type of platform and that perhaps the Canada benefits may not be as significant as what they absolutely must be in Newfoundland.
I ask my hon. colleague to expand a little further about the real necessity for maximization of Canada benefits not just as it affects material procurement, but actual jobs and the spin-off industries that could be created. I know many people say that it is pretty parochial to want to keep as much of the pie from development as one can in one's region when so many people, like those in Atlantic Canada, depend on the good graces of people in central Canada to shift their money and resources to help us out.
I ask my hon. colleague to expand on that so that people from all sides of the House and people watching this debate will have a better understanding as to why it is absolutely essential that the Hibernia project go forward, not just for energy self-sufficiency for Canada, but also for the benefits that could accrue to places like Newfoundland, which have waited for a long time to be fed a full plate in this Confederation.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Dartmouth for that question. I think it is a very pertinent and relevant question, one that is not difficult to address but hard to answer in the limited time that I am sure you will impose, as you are required to do, Mr. Speaker.
I want to review the initial feeling about jobs. As a backdrop to that, I am very proud of representing my constituency of Bonavista-Trinity-Conception, which
is named after the three great bays on the east coast of Newfoundland. There is a lot of distinction in that riding.
Every member represents a distinct area of Canada. There is one distinction that I would rather not have. There is ohe distinction that my constituents would rather not have. In the 62 unemployment insurance regions in this country, my riding is in the region that has the second highest unemployment rate in Canada. Northern Manitoba is the highest, with an unemployment rate of 25.4 per cent. Bonavista-Trinity-Conception encompasses an area where the unemployment rate is over 20 per cent. That gives the backdrop against which I discussed the jobs.
I want to give an indication of what jobs mean in Newfoundland. When we were discussing free trade I remember being involved in a debate with one of my constituents and explaining to him that there is a chance that we would gain a certain number jobs and there was a risk that we might lose some. We did not know. He turned to me and said: "Mr. Mifflin, we can't afford to lose one job in Newfoundland. Not one job".
The last time I checked the figures, there were 79,000 in Newfoundland on unemployment insurance. That is a lot of people. That is almost the total number of people in my riding. I have 92,000 people in my riding. That is shocking.
In the statement of principles there was some anticipation of jobs. I will attribute these statistics to the companies because I think one might want to read something into that. Mobil Oil- they were the leader of the project consortium-said 14,500 person-years of direct Canadian employment would be created during the construction phase out of the total of 21,500 person-years required overall.
They went on to say that indirect and induced employment-that is second and third order jobs-were anticipated to increase the total employment impact for Canada to over 40,000 person-years of which almost 35,000 person-years of the project construction would result in Newfoundland. Thirty-five thousand person-years when one job means so much to so many people is indescribable. TTie impact is fantastic.
The production phase was anticipated to create 1,100 direct permanent jobs and 2,450 indirect permanent jobs for a total of 3,500 permanent jobs for the province of
February 9, 1990

Newfoundland. That was the original initial estimate and they will change, and they have changed.
They have gone down.

They have gone down, indeed. I regret to say that. I agree with my hon. friend that they have gone down. That causes me and all Newfoundlanders concern. I hope it causes all Canadians some concern. We are paying good money for this and we want to get as much as we can out of it.
Do you believe the oil companies when they talk this way? What does that say about the oil companies?

The hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca will recall that I referred to the oil company that actually mentioned these figures. I want to specifically attribute it to the oil companies. I could not do the arithmetic. I did not have the facts with me.
These are all kinds of jobs; they are highly technical jobs, good jobs, and they are jobs that would allow Newfoundlanders and Canadians to compete in other jobs once they are trained for this. The second, third and fourth derivatives of this job creation machine have a tremendous impact and a great potential that we should not minimize in this kind of discussion.
I would say to my hon. colleague from Dartmouth, we are kindred spirits. In fact, we all are when it comes to this. We know the problem in Atlantic Canada. One need only go to any organization, any group of people whether they are church people, fishermen, Liberals, Conservative, NDP and talk about this number of jobs, and you will come away a hero. You are a downright hero. When you talk about a 10 per cent reduction in the number of those jobs it is not as cheerful, but it is still there.
I think I have made my point. I thank the hon. member for giving me the opportunity. I have not spoken to Premier Wells recently on this subject, but I know he is generally in favour of the project. Of course he has some concerns, because it is estimated that we have had a 50 per cent reduction in these jobs. Who knows. It is a long way away. We are looking at production in 1996-1997.
Government Orders
The fact of the matter is we will have the jobs, we will have oil production. There are uncertainties and we have to be patient. But let us move ahead now.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext: There are only a few minutes left in the question and comment period. Guide yourselves accordingly.

Mr. Speaker, in responding to comments by the hon. member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception, I simply want to say that like him, I was very surprised at the remarks made earlier by the hon. member for the NDP on Bill C-44 and the Hibernia project. I can inform the NDP member and the hon. member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception that the government is committed to Bill C-44 and to Hibernia. The Prime Minister will honour the undertaking he made to Newfoundland in 1988 regarding the Hibernia project. The Cabinet is also committed. Members on this side of the House, Mr. Speaker, will, of course, unanimously support Bill C-44, because we realize this project is vitally important to Newfoundland and Eastern Canada.
The project will not only help us to maintain and preserve technology but also to develop new technologies and new types of jobs, and to offer young people in Eastern Canada some interesting opportunities. The hon. member may rest assured that on this side of the House we will be working very hard and very effectively to get Bill C-44 passed as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, I have a piece of paper here that I have to make reference to. I thank the hon. member for that reassurance. I am sure that the morale of my constituents and indeed people from Atlantic Canada, having heard the assurance from the government side, will be raised just a little bit more today. That is not a bad thing for a Friday, after the kind of a dismal week that we have had.
We have just heard some comment on the job creation aspect of this matter. I have talked about the morale aspect of it. After all, we are going to produce oil. It might be expensive oil, but we are indeed going to produce oil. I never like to play off one group against the other, but yesterday in Question Period I heard mention-and I think it was attributed to the hon. minister

February 9, 1990
Government Orders
involved-that over the last five years or a similar period $21.7 billion was given in grants to farmers. I think that is tremendous.
I understand farmers are not eligible for unemployment insurance, but I use that only as a bench-mark to look at the $5.2 billion cost of the project. The oil companies are putting in $1.92 billion. Quite frankly I think they are getting a very good deal. Including federal grants for construction, the guaranteed loan by the federal government, the federal loan to help meet interest payments, the federal loan for contingency, the $95 million from the offshore development fund and perhaps even more, and the $11 million for the provincial offshore technical transfer fund, we are looking at $3,281 billion. That is an awful lot of money. After a couple of hundred dollars I stop visualizing what money is like.
That figure, if compared with $27 billion, is not a bad investment for the kinds of jobs we are looking at in eastern Canada where we are hungry, thirsty and crying out for jobs. I would only hope this will be considered sacred and outside budget cuts and that kind of thing. This is long-term thinking, a long-term project. We cannot afford to have hopes dashed at this time.
I would like to conclude my comments by once again thanking the hon. member from across the floor for his reassurance. I hope the government will continue to reassure us as we go through the procedure of finally getting this bill approved and under way.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to see a new Speaker in the chair today. I will not make any reference to the member for Burlington, but if he were here today he would be proud of the speaker.
I want to start by saying that we should not place this project into an either /or situation. I want to make very clear to members from Newfoundland that it is the history of this country, if we have developed into an economic landscape, to see the wreckage of megaproject after megaproject that has been held out as the single hope for the people of a region to restore their economy.
It happens in British Columbia. It has happened in Alberta. It has happened on the prairies. It happens elsewhere in the regions but not so much in central Canada. I urge my good friend from Newfoundland not to get into the trap that this is the only ray of hope for his province and region. Let us understand that if he falls into that trap, it will become the case of consistent subsidies to large corporations that have walked out of this countiy time after time after time with huge profits and left economic wreckage in the region from which it comes.
Need I cite examples? The heavy water plan was the ray of hope, the morale booster. The people were let down and fibbed to. I do not say they were lied to, Mr. Speaker; they were fibbed to. When we signed British Columbia into Confederation, CPR said that it would keep up passenger service. It was given a 10-mile strip of land across this country. The CPR exploited it, made billions of dollars of profit, abandoned the rail traffic, and taxpayers had to pick it up. They were stuck again.
When I was a younger boy I used to believe it when companies, prestigious people in public life such as politicians, company executives or others, said: "Why, if you just give us a little help here we will create a fortune for this region. We will create jobs. We will do this wonderful thing. Just give us the money, the seed money." Then I heard about free enterprise and I was puzzled about it. Free enterprise, I thought, was the God-given right to lose money or make it. Every time there is a megaproject it is held out as if it is some kind of last hope or beacon. The people's hopes are built up and the large corporations have walked out of this country with the money time and time again.
Money is hard to come by. There is not a taxpayer in this country who does not have a sense of the importance of the Atlantic region. At this point my province is in a bit of an economic uplift. We would like to see some of our taxes go to help the poorer regions. That was our whole consensus in building this country as a confederation of nations. In good times we share with our neighbours; in bad times we expect our neighbours to share with us. No special deals, no favours, just a moral obligation as a nation. There is absolutely no resistance. There is a concern and a willingness to help the Atlantic region. I want to get that on the record clearly.
*
February 9, 1990

In that concern there is absolutely no desire to see the oil companies walk off with the vast amount of money that we are talking about. I have been there. I have seen how the oil companies work. I challenge the Minister of Finance to declare how much the oil companies pay in corporate income tax. In my province of British Columbia, when they were creaming off hundreds of millions of dollars selling natural gas, they did not pay one penny in corporate income tax.
When I was Minister of Finance in that province I exposed them and they took out big newspaper ads attacking me for being nasty and telling people about their private business. Do you know what I said to them? I told the oil companies to stuff it. I was sick and tired, as the leader of a government, seeing those oil companies consistently spread false information that they were good corporate citizens. They were not paying any damn money whatsoever in terms of corporate income tax, but they made a lot of money. They had depletion allowances, write-offs and everything else.
Let us go back to the problem in Newfoundland. I do not want anyone to be a tout or a leading light asking for money for oil companies, but the federal government is prepared to put up $3.8 billion. A little over $1 billion is a direct gift and the rest is in loan guarantees. Good, let's take the money; let's cut the oil companies out and sit down with the good people of Newfoundland and decide what we can do with $3 billion.
Money does not grow on trees. It seems to grow on trees for megaprojects. It seems to grow on trees for big corporations that do not pay their fair share. If the government says there is $3 billion available for Newfoundland, let Newfoundlanders sit down and decide how they can best use that money, not tie it into one huge megaproject that may be a Lorelei. My good friend, the member from Newfoundland, knows what a Lorelei is. The sailors of the past saw that little mermaid out there. They have been away from port, their morale is low, they have other needs and the Lorelei attracts them, and the crash comes.
We have had Loreleis on land in this country time and time again. This is another Lorelei. I want to tell you why it is another Lorelei. First, the premier of the province of Newfoundland, who is a good person, has emerged on the national scene in a dimension which I think has been absolutely positive. Regardless of comments made by
Government Orders
people for political purposes, the contribution made by the premier of Newfoundland, even though he is not of my party, has been an outstanding to nation building and a national debate. I want to go on record as saying that.
The premier of Newfoundland is a guy who tells it as it is. I like that. The premier of Newfoundland is like the former Tory premier with whom I worked, Frank Moores. He is another guy who told it as it was. We were the bookends of the country. Frank Moores fought for his province as a Tory in an outstanding manner and I was proud to know Frank Moores. I do not know Wells, but I am impressed.
I want to tell you what Wells said about this project. He is not going to fib to anybody. He is not going to hold out a Lorelei image. He is telling it the way it is.
Premier Clyde Wells recognized that there is a tremendous amount of public money invested for limited employment. In an interview on October 2, 1989, my birthday, in The Financial Post he said that the number of permanent jobs generated by Hibernia would be about the size of the workforce of two fish plants. He said: "The former government is painted as a saviour. It isn't".
My new good friend, the member from Newfoundland, has pointed out that two fish plants would be welcome in Newfoundland. I agree with him. Let us investigate and find out how much fish is being picked up by National Sea Food, which received federal government grants, in its two trawlers and sent to France to be processed while National Sea Food says: "Oh, my goodness, we don't have enough fish for our own work so we have to close in Canada".
Do you know what I say to that? I am a good living person. I try to be temperate in my language, but when I hear that claptrap from a company that received grants and hand-outs from the federal government to run its ships, moved that fish over to France and closed its plants in Canada, the first thing I would say is: "Look you guys, you got Canadian taxpayers' money. You are irresponsible in moving that fish to France. You give us back every single penny you got plus interest".
I know that it is a difficult problem in Newfoundland. We had the same problem in British Columbia. The buccaneers there have run that government through

February 9, 1990
Government Orders
various forms of Tory administrations, alliances, coalitions and all kinds of deals. It is the same thing.
We have heard not a peep out of this government. We have not heard it say: "Bring that fish back". All we hear is the ministers saying: "Oh, we don't not have enough fish". You are damned right you do not have enough fish. It is being sold in France in ships subsidized by the Canadian taxpayers. You do not hear a word about that, do you? Not a word. All the people in Newfoundland should know it. All the people in Canada should know it.
The same thing is going to happen with this project. I believe the suggestion that it is morale lifting and spreading the good light. However, the best way to be a morale lifter and spread the good light is to tell the people of the region that we have $3 billion and decide what we can best do for ourselves in an indigenous development of our economy and tell the oil companies they can wait on the outside until we decide.
Who did it best? The canny Scots. The canny Scots in Aberdeen were faced with the same deal, but they did not chase the first carrot that arrived. They knew the oil was not going rotten under the sea. It had been there for a long time and it could last a bit longer. The canny Scots have a great word. They say "nay" and then they start talking. I suggest the same approach on this deal: "Nay. Now we will do some talking."
What is in it for us? I want to remind my good friend that the government seems to be able to find money conveniently before elections. It talked about $12 billion for submarines. Do you remember that? Of course we knew it would have been a heck of a lot more. We know what the conventional needs for our armed forces are and our armed forces should get those conventional needs met, but that is a separate story. I represent a great naval base in my area and I am proud to do that.
They find this money for the oil companies and my first response is to give this money to the government and the people of Newfoundland and tell them: "Here is $3 billion, start going right now." Not make work projects so they get their 20 weeks in for unemployment insurance. That is the most insulting kind of development possible. Is that a morale lifter? Is that light at the end of the tunnel? Does that provide dignity and self-respect on a long-term basis? Not at all. The people
of Newfoundland deserve more and they deserve it in a way that makes sense, not as some kind of afterthought as a hand-out to the oil companies.
There are no hand-outs.

Let's talk about hand-outs to the oil companies. You represent the oil industry over there. You cannot even accept the fact that some people who wear turbans are Canadians. I find that disgraceful. I will not even deal with that.
I never said that in my life.
They have as much right to be in the mounted police as anyone else in this country, anyone else.

That is totally irrelevant. I will not
discuss it.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I appreciate the sensitivity of this issue. The hon. member for Calgary Southwest accused my friend from Esquimau-Juan de Fuca of using the term "racist" in reference to her. I was in the Chamber and I believe that that was not a term used.
He indicated I was racist.

That is now history in Hansard, but I do hope that people of any religious persuasion will be permitted to join any civil service capacity that is available in this great country of Canada. I just want to put my position on the record. I think it would be welcome for all minorities to have the same rights in this country.
Who is arguing with that?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Would the hon. member please address the bill before the House?

We will let it rest there, Mr. Speaker. I believe in religious freedom, and we will let it rest there.
I want to comment further on this whole question of a commitment to oil companies.

It's a commitment to the people of Newfoundland.
Government Orders
Well, Mr. Speaker, it is a commitment to oil companies. If we want a commitment to the people of Newfoundland, put this money up for restructuring the economy in Newfoundland. Let me talk about-
There are far better ways to do it.

Yes, far better ways. Let me quote from an article published July 25 in The Financial Times. It is not exactly a newspaper that supports the New Democratic Party. I have never seen an editorial in it supporting us. Should they wish to support us, I would consider welcoming it.
However having said that, let me go on to this. This is an article written by the dean of the faculty of management of the University of Manitoba. He said: "As a regional development scheme the project may have some merit, but not in terms of capital cost per job. Energy is one of the world's most capital intensive industries and, accordingly, is a strikingly expansive vehicle with which to deliver regional employment. Temporary construction jobs in Newfoundland will carry a capital cost in excess of $500,000 per job".
It is hard to figure after a couple hundred bucks, as the member said, but $500,000 will employ a heck of a lot of people.
"Permanent production jobs will carry a capital cost of several million dollars per job. Granted, oil is there, but it would be difficult to find a more expensive way to deliver either oil or jobs in Newfoundland."
Who am I to question the author of this article? All I am suggesting is that if the government has $300 million to put up, put it up and let the oil companies put up their own money. I have seen too many giveaways in the history of this country already. This government is always talking about being frugal and being careful with taxpayers' money, cutting and slashing.
They are the guys who just one week ago gave Boeing another $160 million. They are paying them to take the company off their hands. What kind of business is that? What kind of business enterprise is that in front of farmers or fishermen, to tell them you have to take $160 million of taxpayers' money to pay off Boeing to buy the plant? Dumb-bell economics. It is not so dumb if you are paying the piper who calls the tune. The Tories have represented big business in this county since the incep-

February 9, 1990
Government Orders
tion of their party, and when it comes to welfare for big business, they find new ways to do it every day.
That is the record, Mr. Speaker. As a consequence of that record it is my intention to move an amendment, should I find the appropriate document in front of me. The amendment is seconded by the hon. member for Edmonton East who is an outstanding colleague in this House, probably one of the most articulate spokespersons from western Canada and without a doubt the best representative from Alberta that this House presently has.
I have prepared this amendment with his advice and the help of the Clerk. I move:
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the
word "That" and substituting the following therefor:
"Bill C-44, an act respecting the Hibernia Development Project and to amend certain acts in relation thereto, be not now read a second time, because:
(1)	granting the Project more than $1 billion without securing equivalent equity in the Project for the people of Canada is wrong in principle;
(2)	it fails to contain specific provisions which provide environmental protection measures in connection with the Project; and,
(3)	it fails to contain specific provisions which provide for the creation of job opportunities in relation to the Project".
I commend this amendment to you as soon as I affix my signature.
