Mr. Speaker, I stand in support of this reasoned and reasonable amendment which is asking that Bill C-44, an act respecting the Hibernia development project, be not read a second time at this point, because of three very fundamental principles that are not adequately addressed in it.
The first principle is that there is not a securement of sufficient equity for the government in the project. We have set out in the amendment that granting the project more than $1 billion without securing equivalent equity is wrong in principle.
The amendment also suggests that the current legislation fails to contain specific provisions which provide for environmental protection measures in connection with the project. At a later point in my presentation, I want to outline in more detail why that factor is in itself so critically important to whether this project should or should not go ahead.

February 9, 1990
Government Orders
The last provision is also a very salient point. The current legislation fails to contain specific provisions which provide for the creation of job opportunities in relation to the project.
I would like to start by going to the last point first. I come from an area in British Columbia where, like my colleague from Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca, I have seen the cumulative economic impact, or lack thereof, of many of the megaproject developments which have gone on in our province. I speak of projects such as the Columbia River Power Treaty. In that measure a massive investment of taxpayers' money went into creating cheap power and cheap water for agricultural communities in Washington and Oregon, communities which are now competing with and keeping our agricultural communities out of the market.
Some of these projects are incredibly expensive. Let us look, for example, at the Northeast Coal project that was developed years ago. That project was developed under the British Columbia government of Bill Bennett. It involved millions and millions of taxpayers' dollars to develop the coal fields in the northeastern part of British Columbia.
To begin with, after investing all that money, they even put the hole in the wrong place. Millions and millions of taxpayers' dollars went into the creation of an energy project which saw very little return in terms of actual job creation. Certainly, there were jobs created. But when you look at the cost of capital investment necessary there was a million dollars of capital investment that was necessary to create one long-term job in the Northeast Coal fields.
Now, when we are competing with our Australian counterparts for the Japanese coal market, we find that the Northeast Coal project is not able to recover the costs that we were hoping it would be able to recover when the project was initially started. Millions of taxpayers' dollars have gone to create temporary jobs.
If you took $1 million of capital investment-and that is what it was to create one job in Northeast Coal-and you put that money into the community into, for example, the small business sector you could create 10 times the number of jobs that you could for one long-term job
in the capital intensive industry such as in the energy sector. Some $50,000 to $100,000 of capital investment will create jobs in the small business sector. It will also create ten times the economic spinoff in terms of job creation.
Yes, we believe in job creation and, like my colleague from Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca, I think all Canadians are vitally concerned about what is happening in our Atlantic provinces, in Newfoundland, with respect to the economic difficulties that they are involved in at this time. We want to help out. But I think all Canadians, as well as those residents in the Atlantic provinces, also want to make sure that we get the biggest bang for our buck. That certainly cannot be achieved in capital intensive projects such as we have seen with Northeast Coal in British Columbia or in Atlantic Canada with the Hibernia project.
We want to create the most jobs with the money that we do have available. That is why we oppose this bill. We believe it to be an inefficient means of job creation.
We oppose the bill because here we are utilizing federal money without really consulting the people in the communities about whether or not they have some better ideas about how that money should be put to use in creating jobs that will be around for a few years throughout their communities.
When this bill was first introduced on November 7, my New Democratic colleagues and I issued a series of conditions that we felt should be satisfied in order to win support for the project. My colleague from Edmonton East, who I think has so eloquently spoken on this issue a number of times, dealt extensively with these four conditions in his remarks of December 18.
What are those conditions? I would like to review them veiy briefly.
First, there should be no investment of public money without equivalent equity being held by the Crown. It is a fundamental tenet of economic development that there should be no give-aways of taxpayers' money, be it federal, provincial or otherwise. There should not be any give-aways of public money, unless there is an equity position for the government to be attained.
February 9, 1990

The Alberta government made sure it had equity in its Syncrude project. There is no essential equity of investment for Canadian taxpayers' dollars going into this Hibernia project.
The second principle which I think very important is that there should be guarantees in the agreements among the parties that the production costs will not be subsidized by the public purse now or in the future.
Third, the expenditures by the federal government on research, development and the commercialization of energy alternatives and conservation must be restored to a minimum of the $400 million budgeted for it in 1984.1 think all members of this House would agree that there are great opportunities for job creation in this field, small-scale, community-based projects for energy alternatives which will benefit ordinary people, not only in Newfoundland but throughout this country. This is a very important principle and, when we dive into these megaprojects of exploration opportunities for coal fields and oil fields, we sometimes neglect some of the alternative projects we could be developing.
A fourth important point is that concrete steps and guarantees must be put in place to minimize the environmental impacts of the Hibernia project, as well as any other energy project. This should include the assurance that, within the framework of reducing Canada's carbon dioxide emissions, which are the by-product of burning our fossil fuels, we should be reducing those emissions by at least 20 per cent by the year 2005 to combat the problem that we are experiencing even now. That problem is global warming due to the greenhouse effect caused by the increased concentration of carbon dioxide gases in our atmosphere.
This project is not going to help in that respect. Once again, we are tapping our resource of fossil fuels and utilizing fossil fuel products for our energy sources. It is high time that this government put its money where its mouth is in terms of taking on its supposed commitment to the exploration of energy alternatives, something which will utilize other fuel sources. For example, there is hydrogen which, when combined with oxygen in the process of combustion, produces a very simple by-product which is environmentally harmless-water. Those are the kinds of energy alternatives that we should be
Government Orders
exploring rather than simply blundering again into the utilization of our coal fields and oil reserves.
I think I speak for everybody in my caucus when I say that we take very seriously the recommendations made by the Brundtland Commission. The main thrust of the report of that commission was that any kind of economic development taking place has to go hand-in-hand with the need for sensitive environmental planning, a stewardship to ensure the kinds of economic development that we fund and pursue are in harmony with our environmental objectives.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that economics aside, the Hibernia project does not take that into consideration.
The environmental problems that we are running up against today in Canada and throughout the world are becoming increasingly critical. As I mentioned before, the greenhouse effect brought on in large measure by the use of our fossil fuels is having very significant impacts, on a global scale, on our climatic conditions. One of those conditions is the reduction in available sunlight in photosynthesis for aquatic plants. It is changing in a myriad of ways the whole balance in our biosphere and in the ecosystems throughout the world. The longer we continue to ignore those important problems the greater the ultimate crisis will become.
The points that my colleague from Edmonton brought before this House earlier are reasonable conditions for any energy project that is to be considered. The government could have pursued a bill on Hibernia that did satisfy these sensible and reasonable requests. But it chose not to do so. As a result the projects that have resulted will provide comparatively few jobs. I mentioned before a case where it took a million dollars of capital investment to create one job. When I say that that is not getting the biggest bang for the buck I think we would all agree with that.
Newfoundland needs real economic development. Hibernia could help with that. We do not have any argument in that regard. But that is not likely to happen with this current bill because many of the potential benefits to Newfoundland and Labrador have been squandered and ignored by this current piece of legislation.

Government Orders
I would like to deal with the other principles in the reasoned amendment before the House. However, before I do that I would like to outline or review a bit of the history of the Hibernia project.
It is a project that has been a dizzying roller-coaster of raised expectations and dashed hopes for our Atlantic friends. When the first major oil discovery was made in the Grand Banks back in 1979 the expectation was that Newfoundland would blossom to become what they called at that time the Norway of North America. Unfortunately, the first estimates of the amount of oil contained in the oil fields were soon proved to be much too optimistic, too high.
In 1979, it was estimated that the Hibernia fields contained about 1.8 billion barrels of oil. By 1985, the estimate was in fact much lower. The field is estimated to contain between 800 million and 900 million barrels- nothing to sneeze at but certainly not the great expectations that we had in 1979.
The most recent estimate with respect to the Hibernia reserves has lowered it to between just 500 million and 650 million barrels. We can see that it does not have the great potential we thought it had when the oil fields were discovered initially.
The estimates of the benefits from the project that would have been enjoyed by Newfoundlanders have similarly declined steadily. Initially, Newfoundlanders believed that the province owned this off-shore resource and that it would be used mainly to provide much-needed jobs to boost the Newfoundland economy.
This hope of exclusive provincial ownership and control was dashed by the rulings of the Supreme Court of Newfoundland and the Supreme Court of Canada in 1983 and 1984. Basically, it was ruled that the federal government would have jurisdiction over this off-shore mineral resource.
The Atlantic Accord, a long-term agreement on the joint management of off-shore oil and gas development, was signed in 1985. But, as Newfoundlanders know only too well, the agreement does not change the simple fact that Hibernia will not in itself transform their provincial economy.
On top of the disappointing realization that Hibernia would not be the bonanza that was initially thought,
politicians have repeatedly used the promise of the project, quite frankly, for crass political purposes. They have repeatedly raised the hopes of the people of Newfoundland by making the big glitzy announcements, the deals, strangely enough either just before or during election campaigns. We all know how quickly promises evaporate once an election is over and done with. We all know how quickly those promises have evaporated in the past. You cannot blame people for being a bit reluctant to accept the promises this government has continued to make in terms of its commitment to some of its election goodies.
The project was announced once in 1979. It was announced again in 1982 and yet again in the 1988 federal election when the federal Conservatives made Hibernia an important plank in their Atlantic Canada platform. Each time the impression was given that a final deal was completed, that it was wrapped up, that it was in the bag, that it was just a matter of putting the bells and whistles on it, and this would mean great things for Newfoundland.
This is what the Prime Minister said at the time during a pre-election stop in St. John's, on July 18, 1988:
Hibernia has been the dream of the people of Newfoundland and
Labrador for decades. Ibday, the dream has been realized.
In the midst of the last election campaign on October 6, 1988, the Prime Minister, once again, waxed lyrical about the project, as he is often wont to do. He said: "For me, Brian Mulroney, Hibernia meant a lot more than barrels of oil. Hibernia, to me, was about dignity. Hibernia is about the future, about jobs for our kids. It is about a new tomorrow".
For his part Trade Minister John Crosbie told more than 1,000 invited guests in St. John's that the announcement has nothing to do with politics, it has to do with simple justice. That was in 1988.
I am certain the government will try again somehow to blame the opposition for holding up Hibernia.
I will summarize by making it very, very clear that we in the New Democratic Party are not opposed to the Hibernia project. What we are opposed to is the fact that the federal dollars involved in creating Hibernia could better be spent on a community-by-community basis developing the kinds of projects that Newfoundlanders
February 9, 1990

themselves feel are the best means for economic development and job creation in their province.

Mr. Speaker, in the same context, but perhaps expanding it a bit, I was just wondering if the hon. member could comment on what the effect of this headlong rush into megaproject development, not only Hibernia, but across the country might be in light of the free trade agreement.
My understanding of the free trade agreement is that once we achieve a certain level of export to the United States that level of export then becomes the bottom line of what we have to make available to the Americans in perpetuity through the free trade agreement. For example, if 60 per cent of our production of oil or 50 per cent of our production of gas is committed to the Americans at a certain point in time, then from then on forward that will be the production level.
I found it very interesting when the member commented that we should make incremental kinds of investments in our energy future, including investments in conservation and so on which would benefit Newfoundland communities and all others. Might that not also be a more intelligent way to go about it, rather than at this time rush into a whole series of megaprojects, the bulk of which products go to export? That will place us in a position whereby our non-renewable hydrocarbons will be locked into an export pattern we will not be able to get out of.

Mr. Speaker, I believe the member has posed a very salient question. It is also a very important question in terms of the impact of the free trade agreement on our energy resources.
There is no question that the free trade agreement as is signed and implemented today has far more to do with access to Canada's resources than it has to do with the reduction of tariff barriers. That is why we initially opposed the free trade agreement before it was implemented. That is why we continue to oppose it today.
The fact is that the FTA is really an attempt by our neighbour to the south to access our vital resources, our energy supplies, our electricity and hydro supplies, our water-in fact, the lifeblood of Canada.
Government Orders
The section of the agreement dealing with energy basically says that once contracts have been established for the provision of Canadian energy supplies to U.S. markets and once that trade has taken place, the federal government of Canada or a provincial government loses control of that resource. That is so because in times of energy crisis they can no longer cut back on exported supplies of that energy without cutting back an equivalent amount on our own domestic supplies. That is what is so wrong with that aspect of the trade agreement.
These megaprojects are exploring our resource base and opening up these resources, a major portion of which we know darn well will then be exported to our southern neighbours. Once we have established those export markets, if we have to cut back 10 per cent on our export supply, the free trade agreement says: "You can't cut back on 10 per cent of the export supply to the U.S. unless you cut back an equivalent amount in your own domestic consumption". That means we are losing control and the husbandry of our own natural resources.
In light of that, the development of these megaprojects has to be very seriously questioned indeed.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the hon. member.
I have to say that I have enjoyed the debate today on government participation in megaprojects. It is debated in our small post offices in the Cariboo-Chilcotin. It is debated over office coffee urns, in our beer parlours and at our church socials. It is a subject that is very important to a lot of people in Canada. I do not know that there is anybody wise enough to give the ultimate answer.
The hon. member supports the motion to squash what is considered by the people of Newfoundland to be their opportunity. They want the Government of Canada to help them help themselves. It is easy for people to squash a project that is considered important by people on the other side of the country.
My question for the member is this. There are projects in British Columbia in which the federal government's presence and assistance is necessary. Would the hon. member be prepared to have the federal government also squash the gas line to Vancouver Island and the icebreaker that will be there to assist our shipbuilding industry in British Columbia?

February 9, 1990
Government Orders

Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member has missed a very vital point in my argument. The argument is not to squash the project. The argument is that if we go ahead with it we want some assurances that the federal government has equity in the project. We want some assurances that there are environmental impact assessments done with respect to the project. We want some assurances that the long-term interests of our energy supplies are secured before this project goes ahead.
We want to make sure that the $3.1 billion in investments is used by the people of Newfoundland rather than being squandered away by giving it to the multinational oil companies. We want to assess the rationale for using $1 million in capital investment to create one job, or whether perhaps it makes more sense to take that $3.1 billion and use it in other sectors of the economy where you are going to produce 10 to 50 times the number of jobs for every dollar you spend.
It is a matter of putting the bucks where you are going to get the biggest bang for them. I think that that makes ultimate economic sense.

Mr. Speaker, I have a comment on this amendment. When I look at a copy of it, it seems to me it is there simply to stall this bill. We would like to see the Hibernia bill go to committee. I think there are a lot of technical details in it. We want it to go to committee so we have the opportunity to hear witnesses and to make improvements in this legislation.
The NDP say that they want assurances. We also want assurances. This amendment shows that the NDP members are more concerned with technical details. I think the place to deal with these details is in committee and that is what we would like to recommend because we want to get on with this process which is advantageous to Atlantic Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I want to point out that the member may wish to peruse the exact wording of the reasoned amendment. Nothing in this amendment can, in fact, be dealt with in committee. These amendments are far more than simply housekeeping measures and changes in wording. It changes, in fact, the principle of the legislation. What she calls technical details and housekeeping measures are about whether or not the Canadian taxpayer deserves the right of equity financing
in projects of this sort, or whether we are going to give $3.1 billion holus-bolus to multinational investments.
The amendment is concerned with whether or not there are adequate provisions for environmental safeguards in this project. Every Canadian citizen knows that the major concerns in this country-the major concern globally-are environmental issues. This government has itself given the commitment, at least it has paid lip service to the commitment, that all projects would receive an environmental assessment as to whether or not they should proceed. This is far more than simple housekeeping. The creation of jobs for people in Newfoundland is far more than a simple housekeeping measure.
Megaprojects are capital intensive. They do not create enough jobs for the amount of money spent. Our position is that perhaps there could be other mechanisms by which we get the biggest bang for the buck.

Mr. Speaker, I had actually hoped to catch Your Honour's eye before now, because I wanted to say that I found the recitation of the history of the project that the hon. member was relating to the House a most interesting one. I was hoping that I could invite him to continue with that recitation in the time remaining so that all members might be further enlightened.

Mr. Speaker, you caught me unaware on that one. Because I had summarized somewhat it will take me half a second to go back to where I was before.
We talked about the historical aspect of Hibernia and the number of promises that have been made time and time again by this government in regard to the development of the project.
Let us have a look at what is actually in Bill C-44. In a nutshell, the bill is meant to give the federal government the statutory authority to enter into one or more legally binding agreements based on the statement of principles signed in July, 1988. It sets out how the federal government will spend money on the project.
Mr. Speaker, in the very brief time I have remaining I want to point out that we are talking about a great deal of money. We are talking about $1.04 billion toward capital costs, $1.66 billion in loan guarantees for capital projects, $.175 billion in loan guarantees for temporary financing; $.3 billion is a loan. No cap on the amount contributed as interest. $3,139 billion in taxpayers' money is a lot of money. Is it a wise use of that money?
February 9, 1990

That is all we are asking. Does the legislation that is before us set out a mechanism for the judicious use of federal taxpayers' money?
Let me emphasize once again that we do not oppose Hibernia in principle. We do oppose the fiscal arrangements that are set out in this piece of legislation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It being 2.34 p.m., the House will now proceed to the consideration of Private Members' Business as listed on today's Order Paper.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   EMPLOYMENT JOB-CREATION STRATEGIES

speakeroldname: Mr. Ray Funk (Prince Albert-Churchill River) moved:
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   EMPLOYMENT JOB-CREATION STRATEGIES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of ensuring that federal job-creation strategies emphasize job opportunities that extend beyond the industrial and commercial sectors and include the arts, culture, social and voluntary services, and community-based enterprises.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I think it is quite appropriate that this private members' motion, which I am introducing comes before us on this particular day. It is a day on which we see the contrast of philosophies, with the government promoting, on the one hand, massive investments of billions of dollars in megaprojects. This money will, in large part, end up in the hands of large multinational corporations, for each dollar invested will yield very little in terms of job creation in a region of the country where such job creation is so badly needed. On the other hand, earlier today, we had the Minister of Employment make an announcement with regard to one of the government's major employment creation projects, the Challenge '90 project, which, through a series of smoke and mirrors, ends up being even less of a program than it was before. This program was very useful in communities from coast to coast, communities that every
Private Members' Business
one of us represent. I think it is very appropriate that we address this particular question, on the one hand, a community-based development philosophy and on the other a megaproject-big business type of philosophy.
One of the things that concerns me very much, as a member of this House and as a witness to what is happening to our communities, to our economy and to our country, is that this government seems to be lost in a dark ideological tunnel that seems to have no turns. I find it hard to comprehend why that should be true because, as I get to know members opposite better on a personal basis and work with them in committees and so on and discuss issues with them, I realize that in many ways the partisan differences between us tend to blur when it comes to concern about our communities and interest in local projects and the kind of things that we support from day to day as members of Parliament.
Therefore, it seems incongruous to me that these same members then end up voting and supporting a point of view in a series of legislative initiatives that fly in the face of the kind of work they do and take a great interest in as individual members.
I have come to the conclusion that the government opposite is much less than the sum of its parts. I think there are three basic issues inherent in the question we are addressing today. One is a very fundamental problem with the values this government lives by and which it promotes as being those that Canadians should emulate. It is very much a bottom line orientation towards life, an orientation that says that if you are not part of big business, if you are not the rat race, if your goals are not to get ahead as fast as you can economically, if you are not prepared to get there and elbow your way through different kinds of economic competitive environments, then you do not have a place in society. If you are not turned on by the vision of capital flowing back and forth through capital markets around the world day and night, if you do not follow the stock market very closely, if these things are not of interest to you and if that is not where your life revolves then somehow or other you are a second-class citizen and this government does not really have a role to play in your life.

February 9, 1990
Private Members' Business
It seems especially ironic that the historic Conservative party should end up in that kind of a values vacuum. I had always seen the Conservative party partly that way because my constituency was represented by the late John Diefenbaker, and perhaps because the old British Tory tradition of conservatism respected community life, family life, and applauded local grassroots initiative.
Instead, what we see is a headlong rush into the materialistic type of big business-oriented philosophy that leaves our society not only socially much poorer, but in many ways, spiritually much poorer. Ultimately, it gets us on a environmental treadmill that we will not be able to get off. In fact, it holds within it its own seeds of destruction.
I might comment in that regard on what is happening in eastern Europe. My own family roots are in eastern European. My family was forced to leave the Soviet Union in 1927. If the bankers take our farm away in Saskatchewan, perhaps Mikhail Gorbachev might give our farm back in the Soviet Union, in view of the changes that are happening there.
Nevertheless, I have heard a lot of comments from people espousing neo-conservative, right wing ideas. But what is happening in eastern Europe is, in fact, a sudden conversion to a completely capitalist, free enterprise kind of thinking.
I think that is certainly part of the answer. I know that there people have been very frustrated, as our family was, with the inability of individuals and communities to make their own economic decisions. But there was also a structure evolving in that country that was oriented from the top down, where individuals and communities had no control.
I think that can happen in a private enterprise economy as it did in a communist economy. We are seeing in our country that people are feeling less and less in control of their lives. The values that are driving this culture, the same as they did there-it was called economic materialism-are giving rise to a right wing version of economic materialism that is just as destructive to individuals and communities as the communistic type of economic materialism was in eastern Europe.
Another problem with this government is that it recognizes only two-thirds of the economy and of that two-thirds, it only supports one-third. If you analyze the economy, it has three sectors, not two. There is a corporate business sector, a public sector basically evolving around different levels of government, and then there is a community sector which includes voluntary organizations. They, in turn, include organizations, such as small family-owned businesses, community development corporations and co-operatives; all the kinds of little grassroot local activities that people carry on in the economic sphere. I think that it is just as important, perhaps more important, to help people live in our communities as it is the big government and private sectors. This government has really lost sight of that in spite of the fact that it represents those same communities as I do.
I might also comment that if you look at the economic history of the country those sectors are the ones that are durable in tough times and are the ones that have endured.
The other problem is that this government is proceeding without a full employment policy. The interest rate policies of the Bank of Canada under its Governor, John Crow, make it very clear that fighting inflation by creating exorbitantly high interest rates is much more of a priority to this government than full employment. In fact, the government does not even talk about full employment. It becomes quite clear that the corporate agenda is to force wages down, which it thinks it has to do in order to compete economically in the world, requires high unemployment. In that way people will not make higher wage demands and develop expectations that this government does not want ordinary Canadians to be able to realize. If you look at the successful economies of the world that are competing successfully and are making progress, the economies of western Europe, the economies of Japan and so on, you will see that those economies have very focused emphasis on full employment and on ensuring that everybody has a role to play in the economy.
In fact I have heard it argued that one of the reasons we are having so much trouble financing our social programs and one of the reasons the country is continually clawing back and cutting and making it more and more difficult for a lot of these social programs to survive is because social programs have not been tied to
February 9, 1990

a full employment program. Surely a full employment program is the most successful social program you can have for a great number of people.
I started by mentioning the Challenge program that was introduced today and I would like to return to that as an example of what I am talking about. This program, at least in a limited way, gives young people some opportunity to get experience in the job market. It also gives local communities a source of funding to get some local projects completed and to do interesting things that benefit the communities. But what did we see happen today? There was an announcement, which on the face of it has some merit, about the stay-in-school program. There was a big announcement that it was funded to the tune of $296 million. In much smaller print was the fact that that $296 million was spread over five years and in fact amounted to $60 million a year.
But where did that money come from? The money came out of what is called the SEED program. We have $60 million going toward staying in school this year. We have a loss in the SEED program which was the program available to post-secondary education students. $41.8 million was taken out of that program in the same year-a 35 per cent cut. All that has happened is that high school students are getting some support to stay in school at the expense of university students who will now have to take even bigger student loans, or find jobs in a very tough job market and pay back student loans at exorbitant rates of interest. That is hardly progress.
In the La Ronge region of my constituency, when last year ended, the Challenge Program had applications for $1.2 million of funding, while only $247,000 of funding was available. This left many very frustrated community groups that were not able to complete their projects and a lot of frustrated students. I have talked to many other members who said it was also true in their constituencies. It turned out to be a program that in many ways perhaps turned out doing more harm than good. This is in a constituency where only 23.15 per cent of the people between 15 and 65 are listed as working. In other words, it is a constituency with 77 per cent unemployment, according to Statistics Canada.
I would also like to make some proposals, as I did in my motion, as to how the government might come to terms with its very short-sighted and incomplete approach to job creation.
Private Members' Business
I think what has happened in Quebec has given us a fine example of how encouragement for the arts and culture not only benefits arts and culture and the people who are interested in pursuing those but has also given a real boost to that province as a whole. I am thinking of the self-confidence, not only in the cultural and nationalistic sense that we see arising in the province of Quebec but also of the success in entrepreneurial business areas. It comes from the fact that Quebecers have been able to develop a sense of themselves of which they are proud. I think that comes very much from the support for arts and culture that has happened in that province.
On the other hand what do we see in English Canada? Lately we have seen the CBC cuts which were only the latest in a whole series of cuts to the CBC. I know that a lot of those were designed to trim fat in head office and one thing or another but it also has become very clear at least in my province that a very valuable children's program, Switchback, was cut. That program was produced in Regina and provided employment for local artists and producers and it was the only alternative for children in Saskatchewan to the type of video shows and game shows the commercial networks provide. Part of the CBC cut was the Switchback program. There is also a real threat to the small remote stations that tie the remote communities in this country together.
In my riding we have Emma Lake Art Camp, which is an internationally renowned centre. It is a gathering spot and training ground for artists. For many years it has been struggling to survive as a teaching institution and as a place on the map.
We have local native singers and dancers who cannot get funding to answer an invitation to make a European tour, even though they were judged good enough to perform at the opening of the Museum of Civilization last spring.
A French cultural centre is being proposed which is being bucked by the provincial government and given only lukewarm attention by the federal government. When I looked at the CIC figures, only two out of 294 jobs listed at the local manpower office are in the recreational and cultural areas.
What we have seen is a shift, in accordance with the same value structure, of support for the arts from public institutions to the corporate sector. What that means is,

February 9, 1990
Private Members' Business
first of all, the kind of arts that are supported are those that the corporate sector chooses as being sympathetic to its way of thinking. Second, it perpetrates the centralization of artistic activity of which both public and private institutions are guilty. The big corporations that can afford to fund arts and culture are centred in the big cities and that is where they invest their money. Therefore, the hinterlands of Canada, the small communities, do not benefit. The cultural life of the hinterlands of Canada is stagnating as a result.
A second aspect is the voluntary and social service sectors in this country. Through those sectors, 175,000 people are employed full-time 200,000 man years of voluntary time are donated through the voluntary and social service agency networks. There are all kinds of social needs that need to be met. There are all kinds of people out there who would like to meet them. There are all kinds of studies that say this is a cost-effective way to spend money in terms of return to the economy and multiplier effects in communities and so on. But yet, what do we see? We see large cuts in transfer payments that funded those kinds of programs at that level. We saw a 15 per cent cut in Secretary of State programs last year federally. We are warned of even bigger cuts this year. We saw cuts to the ODA programs.
Again, local initiatives are being left begging, while megaprojects and big business get their way with this government.
The last point I would like to raise is that of community based enterprises. This country has a proud history of development of co-operatives and community development organizations. We are renowned world-wide for this ability. People come here to do research on how to start local grassroots enterprises. But when we see the programs coming out of this government like the CAED program and the aboriginal economic program, when you look at our regional development programs, WDO, look at community futures, when you look at all of these programs, community development organizations and co-operatives take a seat so far back that you cannot even see them from the front. I know that many people who work with these programs are very frustrated by the fact that guidelines are written in such a way that these kind of locally based initiatives find it very difficult, first
of all, to make it through all the hoops and the feasibility studies that it takes to get money.
Second, so often the criteria involved make it impossible for them to access this money. Again, we have a situation where those who really do not need the money can get it, and those who do need the money cannot.
The last point I would like to raise is the whole question of the environment. There is a new employment for local communities opening up in the environmental area; monitoring the environment, cleaning up the mess we made before; participating in local energy development programs. The kind of things that all of us recognize are the wave of the future and would operate best on a local community basis.
In closing, I would like to call on this government to do three things. One is recognize that a third community based sector does exist in this country and does deserve support.
Second, the third sector is the most cost effective, the most positive way to develop local communities and, in fact, to develop the economy. Third, I would like the government to recognize that life is more than being part of the international, big business rat race. I would like members of this government to support this motion and to make the point that we do recognize the value of community life. We do recognize that locally based initiatives are worth supporting.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Edwards (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   EMPLOYMENT JOB-CREATION STRATEGIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with care to what my hon. friend said. I think that the late great John Diefenbaker would not be ashamed of him at all. I think he has done his homework. Mr. Diefenbaker would not agree entirely with his ideological point of view, but I think he would respect the work that the hon. member put into his thoughts and into his speech.
As the hon. member appreciates what I am about to say, he will find himself returning to his natural roots of conservativism. Perhaps even his riding will some day under his leadership do the same. I would invite the hon. member some day to come with me into the bosom of the Department of Communications where, just the other day, I spent several hours discussing cultural initiatives in the provinces of Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta. I recognize the centralist tendency that he alludes to. It is one that I have been concerned about as well. I can assure him that there are those of us in government who
February 9, 1990

are working to combat that natural tendency of a system such as ours seems to have built into it.
The Canadian Jobs Strategy introduced in September, 1985 focuses on training and development in the Canadian labour market through the six programs created by the strategy. Many organizations and individuals in the cultural sector have benefited from the opportunity to develop their skills and enjoy newly created employment possibilities. There is no question that the cultural sector is of great importance socially and economically in the life of our country. It is the fourth leading creator of employment. Our cultural industries, including broadcasting, directly employ more than 185,000 Canadian and are one of the fastest growing sectors of our economy.
In terms of social significance, our nation's creators have won international recognition and secured our reputation as a vibrant, creative and vital people. Artists form the cornerstone of our distinct identity as Canadians. As the Minister of Communications so aptly noted in outlining the status of the artist's initiative recently before the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture a society without artists is a society without identity.

The Canadian Jobs Strategy acknowledges the cultural sector's contribution to our society. Interested members of the cultural community can apply for assistance offered under any of the following programs included in the Strategy: Skill Investment, Job Entry, Job Development, Skill Shortages, Innovations, Community Futures and summer employment programs for young people.
Employment and Immigration Canada gives a broad definition of the cultural sector which includes visual arts, literature, interpretative arts, heritage activities including museums, art galleries, archives and libraries, and our cultural industries including radio and television, film, video, sound recording and editing.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure you will agree that the broad range of activities that can be supported by the Canadian Jobs Strategy reflects a sincere and substantial commit-
Private Members' Business
ment by the government to Canada's cultural development.
I would like to mention some specific initiatives that are now a possibility in the cultural sector, through the financial support of the Jobs Strategy.
Skill Investment provides assistance in training workers affected by technological or market change. They are helped to re-train or acquire new skills.

In Alberta, a sound production company is developing the music engineering and studio technical skills of employees under the small business training option.
In-Prince Edward Island, an art gallery intern at the Confederation Centre for the Arts was able to attend a three-week Banff School of Management program with assistance toward tuition and transportation.
In Ontario, an association representing workers in the Canadian film industry, including self-employed workers, is developing a training trust fund with Employment and Immigration Canada which will enable its members to upgrade various technical skills.
The objective of the Job Entry Program is to assist youth and women having difficulty making the transition from school or home to the labour market. A project in Thunder Bay for youth from small communities who have an interest in the arts is providing training in arts management and entrepreneurial skills, along with practical experience in arts organizations.
In Fredericton, New Brunswick, 20 women have been trained to become archivists. Some projects have provided training and work experience for people wanting to be library assistants and apprentice theatre managers. Other projects are developing skills in broadcast sales, marketing and journalism.
Through another Canadian Jobs Strategy initiative, the Job Development Program, people have been hired to work on projects to develop the management, production, technical or curatorial skills which will qualify them for long-term positions. For example, the Aerospace Museum of Calgary is training eight individuals to repair and rebuild three World War II aircraft and set up an aviation library.

February 9, 1990
Private Members' Business
In Sioux Lookout, three native people are being trained for work in the media. Dance companies, theatre companies, orchestras, art galleries, cultural centres and libraries are among the many other organizations benefiting from this imaginative enterprise.
The Skill Shortages Program provides assistance when employers are unable to find workers with occupational skills which have been designated, nationally or regionally, as being in short supply.
With funding from the Skill Shortages Program, the Canadian Opera Company is managing a three year training program for opera singers, fund raising consultants and technical personnel. People are being trained in several other artistic and administrative occupations in regions where shortages exist.
Prince Edward Island, arts administration and video production skills are being developed by an art gallery, arts centre and video production company.
In Alberta and Nova Scotia, arts administrators and stage managers have been trained.
Another component of the Canadian Jobs Strategy, the Labour Markets Innovations Program, is designed to assist individuals and groups to develop and implement innovative responses to particular market situations. Participation is open to groups or individuals anywhere in Canada.
Examples of innovations projects are the Dancer Transition Center, which assists professional dancers to move from active performance into a second career; the Academy of Canadian Cinema and Television's national apprenticeship program for young Canadian film makers; the Festival of New Canadian Plays, being developed by Alberta theatre projects, which aims to demonstrate to potential corporate investors the viability and importance of Canadian plays; and a Musical Performance and Communication Project designed to improve employment prospects for musicians.
These programs represent a substantial investment in our future by the Government of Canada. They are providing the training which the talented men and women in our cultural sector need to improve their skills.
They also enable young people to enter demanding professions which today call for a high level of training and expertise.
Earlier this year, the government announced that it intended to build on the success achieved by the Canadian Jobs Strategy. A commitment was made to maintain annual funding for the strategy at the present level of $1.8 billion. In addition, with the announcement of a new labour force development strategy, and the reallocation of $1.3 billion in unemployment insurance expenditures, the sum of $800 million was committed to assist in upgrading the skills of the labour force. These additional funds offer new opportunities for the cultural sector.
The art of promoting our culture and unique identity should not fall on the shoulders of the Minister of Communications alone. It is the responsibility of all of us who take pride in calling ourselves Canadians.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   EMPLOYMENT JOB-CREATION STRATEGIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the member opposite just read out an impressive list. I find that a little sad because it is easy to take select examples and say we are doing good things. The government does have some good programs.
What is missing, obviously, is an overall view of where our economy and society is going with a comprehensive meshing of policies. We on this side of this House have expressed our concerns about the Labour Force Development Strategy and various other elements of economic policies of the government because they do not seem to be leading anywhere.
I want to discuss the problems as I see them in the context of this motion before the House today. This morning's announcement by the Minister of Employment and Immigration typified the lack of fundamental understanding on the part of the government of some of the problems the country faces, businesses face and some of the problems our young people face. It is reflective also of the unwillingness of the government to commit the resources in order to invest in the future of the economy and the people of Canada in the most productive way for our economic future.
First, the minister takes money from the summer jobs program for young people, money which helps with their
February 9, 1990

education and is vital to our economy. She then puts it into programs to keep young people in high school.
While it is extremely crucial that our young people stay in school and get the kind of education they need, there is no recognition by the government of why young people drop out of school. There is one fundamental factor. If you grow up in a poor household in Canada you are four times as likely to drop out of high school before you have the education you need.
That indicates to me is in fact that poverty is a fundamental cause of school dropouts. It does not make sense to take money from one group of people who are pursuing their education to give it to others so that they will stay in school without recognizing the reason they are dropping out of school is poverty. At the same time, it is cutting back the kinds of transfer payments to the provinces that ultimately deal with the fundamental problem of poverty which keeps people dropping out of school. It just does not make any sense. It is patchwork at its worst.
One-fifth of money allocated to keeping young people in school is going to go to the information programs, which is propaganda about what a wonderful job the government is doing and which provides healthy contracts for friends of the government. That is not what our young people need.
I want to talk about the Community Development Initiatives. I think it is a great benefit when one comes into this House to have been in touch with what happens in communities, with the dynamics of communities and the strengths of communities. I had this experience through nine years in municipal government, as have many of my colleagues in the House. This experience allows one to know the strength of communities and to bring into play all the resources of a community to resolve problems such as high unemployment, untrained people, poverty in our communities, and to put all those strengths to work to create solutions which will work because they are developed by the people of a community who know their needs best.
We see elements in the government's current programs that not only do not support it, but militate against that happening. We see a requirement that somebody be
Private Members' Business
out of work for six months and on unemployment insurance before they can get into training programs. That only allows people six months to sink further and further into the concept that they cannot do anything for themselves, that they are incompetent and incapable. When they finally enter a training program with those attitudes, reinforced by six months of unemployment, it is no wonder they do not do as well as they might.
This year several programs in my own community were held up for up to a year because the government, instead of trying to put back in money that it has taken out of training programs and job creation programs, was waiting for the provinces to come up with the money. Programs that were under way and staffed had to close for a year while the government made up its mind whether it was or it was not going to fund them.
Resources continue to be depleted to those programs. Now we are turning to the unemployed and asking them to give up money required for food and shelter for then-families, to give up that money which is essential in order to pay for training and make up for the cuts the government has made over the last number of years.
The Challenge '90 program was cut back last year and it is getting cut back again. What was the effect of that?
The effect of that in my own riding and, I am sure across the country, was that extremely worth-while projects were cut. Many of these programs were operated by volunteer organizations which created jobs for young people and gave them a sense of commitment to their community and a stake in their community. These were programs that helped young children in poverty to have a worth-while summer experience, to feel that they were were worth while so maybe they will grow up and stay in school instead of dropping out.
Voluntary organizations produce up to 10 times the value of the dollars we put into them. That is not true of money we put into businesses. Often we are just paying for an employee the business would have hired in any case. Voluntary organizations can give a young person or anybody a work experience that involves them in their community, that gives them a commitment to then-community and makes them see that education is rele-

February 9, 1990
Private Members' Business
vant, that it has concrete results for society and for their own neighbours and friends.
These are the sorts of programs that we should be funding and which are especially important now when cut-backs to voluntary organizations are rampant and when volunteers are not able to function. There are still volunteers, but they still need paper to mail things out and still need the ability of staff people to support the their efforts. When those are missing we are losing a lot of the value of our voluntary organizations.
I want to expand the discussion because it really is a bigger question than job development, job-creation projects or training projects. It is a question of those much larger multibillion dollar programs that the government has, theoretically, to support employment and job creation in this country. But again today we see unemployment on the rise.
Let us consider the billions of dollars that go out through the Economic Development Corporation to support trade and employment in this country. Are these really the most valuable ways in which to use those dollars? We have seen in recent months serious reasons to question the way in which the Federal Business Development Bank theoretically helps with business development and job creation. It seems to have forgotten that its role is business development, not building development. These are examples of wrong policy directions.
On the other hand, we can look at other more positive directions, other things that are perhaps more worthwhile initiatives for us to invest in. We know that housing and housing renovation has a nine-to-one spinoff in terms of job creation for every dollar invested in it. We know that municipal infrastructure, roads, sewers and water, not only serve the health and safety of Canadians and reduces environmental damage through transportation, but also have a veiy healthy spinoff rate in terms of jobs per dollar invested.
We know that arts and culture, dollar for dollar, is the most labour intensive employment in the country. That is obviously a good way to invest our money if all we are interested in is in job creation, and yet we have the additional benefits of an enrichment of our social and cultural life. Again, instead of support of those industries which naturally produce jobs without any artificial infusion, we see the reduction of funds.
I want to reiterate that the official opposition has a very strong belief in the role of the individual in society and the importance of government supporting and creating an environment where each individual can develop his or her own talents, contribute to society and benefit from that contribution. We simply believe that there must be a comprehensive review of the whole scope of job creation, investment in employment, investment in corporations, and investment in education.
While the motion is a worth-while one, it is only one part of what we need to be looking at as a society. What is good for us as a society is also what is good for job creation and for our economy.
.(1515)

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   EMPLOYMENT JOB-CREATION STRATEGIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand and respect the hon. member's interest in the Canadian job creation strategies and training opportunities. I appreciate the member's concern about finding ways to increase participation in our economy, especially by those Canadians who live in small communities and who work in our arts and culture sectors or social and voluntary services. My hon. colleagues will address these particular issues.
I share the hon. member's desire to build a strong and competitive Canada, through the creation of jobs. I would like to remind him that this government is not a stand pat government. We have always recognized the folly of complacency. We have repeatedly pointed out that if Canada ever adopted a passive approach to job training in this highly competitive world, that strategy would serve as an invitation for disaster.
We have repeatedly warned that the demands of a constantly changing and interdependent global economy must never be underestimated. We have always maintained that the failure to preserve a competitive workforce would have dire consequences for Canada's economic prospects. That is why we have dedicated more dollars to job training and skill enhancement than any government in the history of Canada. That is why we have replaced the hodgepodge of job-creation schemes with a comprehensive plan designed to prepare the Canadian workforce for the challenges of the 21st century.
This government is not in the business of cobbling together short-term make-work projects. That was the traditional approach to job creation.
February 9, 1990

While the quick-fix has at times provided monetary comfort, the relief experienced has too often proven ephemeral and fleeting. Instead, we have adopted a different long-term strategy, a strategy that addresses unemployment and labour market dislocations with an eye to establishing prolonged stability.
I would like to point out to the hon. member that if he carefully examines our programs and policies, he will quickly see that the training we provide is relevant to local conditions and he will find that our training efforts are designed to produce permanent jobs that are in demand now and will be in the future.
I am proud to state unequivocally that the federal government has provided consistent leadership in helping Canadians prepare for the labour market of the 1990s. In September 1985 we launched the Canadian Jobs Strategy after intensive consultation with the provinces, business and labour. Since then this strategy has helped more than 400,000 people each year receive the training they need for tomorrow's jobs.
Unlike previous programs, the Canadian Jobs Strategy is decentralized, relying on people who understand local conditions to come up with solutions that best suit their needs. It places an emphasis on co-operation with the private sector at the local level and offers a mix of tools and programs that has provided a unique and integrated approach to the labour market.
Within the Canadian Jobs Strategy, there is the necessary flexibility and range of activities to allow the government to address the specific needs of the sector identified in this motion: community based enterprises, the arts and culture sector, social and voluntary services.
To point to the arts sector by way of example, there is room within the CJS to support the Dance Transition Centre and a musical performance program. Best of all, CJS has an excellent record in helping those who are on the margins of the labour force and who are most in need. Because of this, I can assure my colleague that our work through the Canadian Jobs Strategy will continue.
Although we recognize the importance of maintaining the income support benefits of the unemployment insurance program, we are still moving toward more active
Private Members' Business
programs of skill development and relevant career training. For example, with Bill C-21 we propose to make the unemployment insurance system more flexible and to use UI moneys to help claimants get back to work faster. That is what Canadians want most.
Last spring we announced a Labour Force Development Strategy that builds on CJS and places a major emphasis on skill development and employment training. The Labour Force Development Strategy is a comprehensive, wide-ranging formula for improving the function of Canada's labour force, and it contains measures geared specifically to help communities found in areas such as the one the hon. member represents.
These measures include strengthening the Community Futures Program and the Industrial Adjustment Service, or IAS. Both programs will receive additional financing under the Labour Force Development Strategy. Community Futures, for example, will see its 1990-1991 budget increase by $50 million to $198 million, while the Industrial Adjustment Service allocation is being doubled from $15 million to $30 million.
I would like to point out that IAS, the Industrial Adjustment Service, has inspired countries from all over the globe. Recently a delegation from Hungary visited Employment and Immigration Canada's headquarters to learn more directly how IAS operates. The Americans have also turned to us for guidance. They searched the world for an effective, industrial adjustment program, and the one they finally settled on was ours.
Once again, in human resource development, we are leading the way, but the task of building a labour force of tomorrow is not ours alone. It also involves the efforts and the co-operation of business, industry and labour. All these major sectors must be willing to make a major investment in Canadian workers if we are to remain relevant in the international economic arena.
Canadian workers are well aware of the importance of training in today's economy. In 1988, Decima did a survey and found that half the respondents said that they would reduce their wage demands in return for additional training.

February 9, 1990
Private Members' Business
In conclusion, our challenge is to address this desire to learn and upgrade skills. I believe that the Labour Force Development Strategy will meet this challenge. It is instituting an unprecedented level of co-operation among business, labour and the government in the interests of building a competitive and relevant labour force. We want everyone to take advantage of the many new opportunities that the Labour Force Development Strategy offers. I am confident Canada will grow and prosper in the next century because of the commitment that we and our partners are ready to make today.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   EMPLOYMENT JOB-CREATION STRATEGIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to talk on this topic today.
I was interested in the motion that the hon. member from Prince Albert-Churchill River proposed. I have to say that I was disappointed that he did not spend as much time talking about culture and the arts as I expected. He diverted quite a bit into the whole political spectrum of megaprojects and other forms of economic assistance to the various communities and regions of our country.
I can divert, for a couple of seconds, by indicating that it is not a matter of making choices between megaprojects for Newfoundland or any other region, but in place of municipal programs it is a matter of a wise and judicious balance between the two. The regions of Canada have legitimate aspirations whether it is us in British Columbia, the people from the good province of Saskatchewan with their aspirations, or the people from the maritimes with their real needs now and their aspirations.
What the member was alluding to was the current bill and the plans the government has to try to provide assistance to that region's aspirations, and I think quite legitimately. Any government that does not consider the needs and the wants of the regions of Canada is one that is going to be in trouble. Equally, of course, the aspirations of the communities of this country must be considered. The area I represent, Cariboo-Chilcotin, is comprised of many of these small communities. It is essential that we as a government and as members of parliament keep in mind what those aspirations are and make sure that we balance the dollars, our time and our attention with those needs.
Obviously government cannot provide everything for everybody. Somebody in my riding said the other day that it is only children and socialists who feel that we can have all of the goodies and not pay the price. Obviously, if we want the goodies we have to pay the price. Government, especially government in these times, is a body that has to make very difficult choices. All we can do is hope we are making wise choices and decisions, all of which must be fiscally responsible.
But heaven protect any government or any member of parliament who, in his eagerness to establish the economic base that is necessary, forgets that we have to be fed and clothed before we can really enjoy an art show, watch a presentation in a theatre or enjoy a hockey game. The government must spend the predominance of its time ensuring that the basic economic strength of our communities and our regions is solid and strong, that the people are working and that their basic needs are met.
Once they are met and we ignore for any length of time whatsoever the needs of the cultural and artistic communities or the interest in their communities, we do so at our peril. I made a mistake in one meeting with a constituent who I hope will become a very good friend. She felt that I was not paying due attention to her interest area which was the arts. She is a very artistic lady and spends untold hours daily and weekly in supporting the artistic endeavours of her community.
She took me on and did so quite properly, to make sure I understood that the needs of that community were real and, more important, that job opportunities, vacancies and potential in those areas were real. I have to admit that I had not given attention to it prior to that meeting. Since then I have been astounded by the many opportunities that exist, the economic incentives and push that the arts and culture communities perform in the Canadian economy. Listening to the debate today I have gained a perspective of several other members in this area.
What we are talking about in the arts and culture community are more than 185,000 people currently working there. They make their living in the performing arts, theatre, music, opera, dance and the visual arts. One that is very important to my area of the country is the heritage sector. Quite often we do not think of this as being one of the cultural artistic areas but it is. It is
February 9, 1990

composed of our museums, galleries, archives and libraries.
Then there is the high-tech sector. Of course high tech is very in at the present time and, despite the added emphasis now on television, we cannot forget the radio to which a person my age has spent so many hours listening. It is still an effective medium, not only for broadcasters but in particular for the performances of music and artistic expression.
There are many people in my Chilcotin wilderness who use their battery radios to tune in to the only station where they can get their dose of arts and culture, or after their basic needs have been satisfied through the CBC air waves and the many fine programs that are put on over the radio and on television.
Another area that is fairly important to the Cariboo- Chilcotin is that of crafts. It is one that I have not heard mentioned here today, but to our aboriginal peoples it is one that is going to become more and more important. It will be important for the government to make sure that we give full consideration to and understand the potential of this area. It is not just in their carving and their art. There is a huge market developing now for the art work.
On a recent trip to Asia, I noticed that business people who have an appreciation for art were commenting on how in at least the larger cities of Asia they were starting to show a greater appreciation for the aboriginal art from Canada, as well as from the United States. They now have carvings and jewellery that are not only beautiful but are creating a meaningful livelihood for so many of the artists who can communicate through that medium. We are seeing more and more of their native dancing and their native theatres. I am sure that form of participation and development in our native aboriginal communities will continue to be a major factor in the arts and culture of Canada.
Private Members' Business
Arts and culture are not just in the big cities, even though we tend to think of seeing ballet in the major cities and symphony orchestras perform principally in the major cities. The small communities of Canada are also recipients of the efforts of the people who work in arts and culture.
On one of my recent trips home-actually it was in Quesnel-there was a visiting group from Montreal, a fine francophone group of musicians, world-renowned percussionists who were performing for the people of the Quesnel area. This was in the Cariboo, the hinterland of Canada. One of the artists was commenting on it. He said: "All of the world-renowned artists play in Paris, in New York, in Montreal, in Hong Kong, all of the major centres". He singled us out in Quesnel and said: "We feel unique because very few of those world-renowned artists have played in Quesnel." We did appreciate it in Quesnel, and one of the benefits that the Government of Canada is able to provide to the small communities is to assist in such endeavours.
On a closing note, I will add that in small towns and big towns in Canada 13.5 million people have been participating in the arts and cultural community. There are more funds brought in from people watching the arts than the total for professional hockey, professional football, as well as baseball.
